commands.name: /add-dir
commands.summary: Adds an additional working directory for file access in the current session.
commands.what:
Adds an additional working directory for file access in the current session. Most .claude/ configuration is not automatically loaded from the added directory.

You can later resume the session from the added directory with --continue or --resume.

whenGood.title: Briefly access a second codebase without switching sessions
whenGood.example: /add-dir ../shared-lib — look up a utility function from the shared lib while continuing work in the main project

whenGood.title: Pull in reference files from a neighboring folder while keeping the prompt cache intact
whenGood.example: /add-dir ../design-tokens — make design tokens available as reference for a styling task

whenBad.title: Wanting to permanently switch to another project with its own CLAUDE.md
whenBad.why: /add-dir does not automatically load the .claude/ configuration of the added directory
whenBad.alternative: use /cd instead — it picks up the target folder's CLAUDE.md and moves the session into its project storage

commands.name: /advisor
commands.summary: Turns the Advisor tool on or off, which brings in a second model for consultation at key moments in a task.
commands.what:
Turns the Advisor tool on or off, which brings in a second model for consultation at key moments in a task.

Accepts opus, sonnet, fable (from v2.1.170), or a full model ID. Without an argument, a picker opens. Requires Claude Code v2.1.98 or newer.

whenGood.title: Bring in a stronger model for a second opinion before a risky architecture decision
whenGood.example: /advisor opus — get a second opinion before implementing a database migration

whenGood.title: Cut costs in a long loop by combining a cheap executor with an advisor consulted only when needed
whenGood.example: /advisor sonnet — as advisor for an automation loop otherwise running on haiku

whenBad.title: Leaving it on for every trivial small task
whenBad.why: each advisory round costs extra tokens/time with no benefit for routine work
whenBad.alternative: open /advisor with no argument and turn it off, re-enable only at real decision points

commands.name: /agents
commands.summary: Manages subagent configurations.
commands.what:
Manages subagent configurations.

From v2.1.198, /agents just shows a hint to ask Claude directly to create/manage subagents, or to edit .claude/agents/ or ~/.claude/agents/ yourself. Up to v2.1.197, the command opened an interactive management interface.

whenGood.title: Ask Claude to create a new subagent configuration
whenGood.example: /agents, then: "create a subagent for database migrations for me"

whenGood.title: Review existing subagent definitions before adjusting them in the current project
whenGood.example: /agents to be pointed to .claude/agents/

whenBad.title: Expecting an interactive management UI
whenBad.why: since v2.1.198, /agents only shows a hint instead of an interactive UI
whenBad.alternative: edit .claude/agents/ or ~/.claude/agents/ directly in an editor

commands.name: /autofix-pr
commands.summary: Starts a Claude Code web session that watches the current branch's pull request and automatically pushes fixes for CI failures or reviewer comments.
commands.what:
Starts a Claude Code web session that watches the current branch's pull request and automatically pushes fixes for CI failures or reviewer comments.

Detects the open PR via 'gh pr view'; a prompt can be passed to give different instructions (e.g. only lint/type errors). Requires the gh CLI and access to Claude Code on the web.

whenGood.title: Let an open PR run unattended against CI failures
whenGood.example: /autofix-pr only fix lint and type errors — after pushing a PR, while working on something else

whenGood.title: Have reviewer comments automatically turned into fixes
whenGood.example: /autofix-pr address all review comments from the last review round

whenBad.title: Changes haven't been pushed as a PR yet
whenBad.why: the command detects the PR via 'gh pr view' and needs Claude Code on the web access — with no open PR it finds nothing
whenBad.alternative: commit/push normally and open a PR with gh pr create first, then run /autofix-pr

commands.name: /background
commands.summary: Detaches the current session from the terminal and lets it keep running as a background agent, freeing up the terminal.
commands.what:
Detaches the current session from the terminal and lets it keep running as a background agent, freeing up the terminal.

With a prompt argument, one final instruction is sent before detaching. Monitor via 'claude agents'. Alias: /bg.

whenGood.title: Free up the terminal while the session keeps running in the background
whenGood.example: /background

whenGood.title: Give one last instruction before detaching
whenGood.example: /background run the tests one more time before you go

whenBad.title: Want to watch the result synchronously
whenBad.why: /background detaches the session from the terminal right now - if you want to see the answer directly, detaching offers no benefit.
whenBad.alternative: just wait in the running session

whenBad.title: Side task with inherited context in parallel with the main session
whenBad.why: /background detaches the entire session, not just a sub-task.
whenBad.alternative: /fork

commands.name: /batch
commands.summary: Orchestrates large changes in parallel across the entire codebase: researches, splits the work into units, and has subagents implement them.
commands.what:
Orchestrates large changes in parallel across the entire codebase: researches, splits the work into units, and has subagents implement them.

[Skill] Breaks the work into 5-30 independent units and presents a plan; once approved, a background subagent starts per unit in an isolated git worktree, implements, tests, and opens a pull request. Requires a git repository.

whenGood.title: A large change that splits into many independent units across the whole codebase
whenGood.example: /batch rename the legacy HTTP client to the new SDK across all 15 services

whenGood.title: A migration where each unit should get its own PR and be tested in parallel
whenGood.example: /batch migrate every module from CommonJS to ESM

whenBad.title: A small task touching one or two files
whenBad.why: the planning phase plus isolated worktrees and per-unit PRs are pure overhead for a small task
whenBad.alternative: use a normal prompt or a single subagent instead of /batch

whenBad.title: No git repository present
whenBad.why: /batch requires a git repository for the isolated per-unit worktrees
whenBad.alternative: run 'git init' first, or make the change manually without /batch

commands.name: /branch
commands.summary: Creates a branch of the current conversation from this point, to try a different direction without losing the history so far.
commands.what:
Creates a branch of the current conversation from this point, to try a different direction without losing the history so far.

Automatically switches to the new branch; the original is preserved and reachable via /resume. For a side task on a background subagent instead of switching yourself: /fork.

whenGood.title: Try an alternative solution path from the current point
whenGood.example: /branch

whenGood.title: Explore a fundamentally different direction and keep working there yourself
whenGood.example: /branch try server-side instead of client-side rendering

whenBad.title: Side task should run in the background in parallel
whenBad.why: branch vs fork: branch switches you into the new branch yourself - for a side task with inherited context running in the background, /fork is meant for that.
whenBad.alternative: /fork

commands.name: /btw
commands.summary: Asks a quick side question without adding it to the main conversation.
commands.what: Asks a quick side question without adding it to the main conversation.

whenGood.title: Ask a quick side question without loading up the main context
whenGood.example: /btw what does the --frozen-lockfile flag do? — while mid-way through a feature session

whenGood.title: Clarify an unrelated question without branching the ongoing conversation
whenGood.example: /btw is there a Windows equivalent for this bash command?

whenBad.title: The answer will be needed later in the main context
whenBad.why: /btw does not add the question and answer to the main conversation
whenBad.alternative: ask as a normal message in the main chat; for a completely new topic use /clear for a fresh start instead

commands.name: /cd
commands.summary: Moves the session to a new working directory.
commands.what:
Moves the session to a new working directory.

The conversation's prompt cache is preserved: the new directory's CLAUDE.md is appended as a message instead of rebuilding the system prompt. The session is moved to the new directory's project storage, so --resume/--continue will find it there. Asks for trust the first time a directory is used. Can be restricted/disabled via 'Cd' permission rules. For access to an additional directory without moving: /add-dir. Requires Claude Code v2.1.169+.

whenGood.title: Permanently move to the next project whose CLAUDE.md should apply from now on
whenGood.example: /cd ../other-project — continue the session fully in the new project

whenGood.title: Store the session in the target folder's project storage so --resume finds it there
whenGood.example: /cd ~/work/client-b before starting the next task

whenBad.title: Just briefly need a file from a neighboring folder while the main project stays active
whenBad.why: /cd fully switches the session instead of just adding access
whenBad.alternative: use /add-dir to access the extra directory without moving

commands.name: /chrome
commands.summary: Opens the settings for 'Claude in Chrome'.
commands.what:
/chrome opens the settings for the connection between Claude Code and the "Claude in Chrome" browser extension. From there you check the connection status, reconnect the extension, choose between multiple connected browsers, or enable Chrome by default for future sessions.

According to the docs, this requires a direct Anthropic subscription (Pro, Max, Team, or Enterprise) and signing in via /login; with a plain API key or a long-lived token from claude setup-token, the integration stays disabled. The feature isn't available via third-party providers like Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud, or Microsoft Foundry, nor under Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL). Supported are Google Chrome, Microsoft Edge, and other Chromium browsers like Brave, Arc, Vivaldi, and Opera.

You start actual browser control with the --chrome flag or by simply asking Claude directly in the prompt.

whenGood.title: Check connection status before a browser task
whenGood.example: Run /chrome and check that 'Status: Enabled' and 'Extension: Installed' are shown before Claude tests in the browser.

whenGood.title: Enable Chrome permanently
whenGood.example: Open /chrome and choose 'Enabled by default' so the --chrome flag is no longer needed going forward.

whenBad.title: Free-plan account without a direct subscription
whenBad.why: According to the docs, /chrome requires a direct Anthropic subscription (Pro, Max, Team, or Enterprise); the integration stays disabled with a plain API key or third-party provider.
whenBad.alternative: Switch to a Pro, Max, Team, or Enterprise plan and sign in via /login.

whenBad.title: Just having a webpage read or summarized
whenBad.why: /chrome only opens the extension's settings; simple reading or searching the web doesn't require visible browser control.
whenBad.alternative: Ask Claude directly in the prompt to read a URL or search the web — Claude uses built-in web tools for that, no dedicated slash command needed.

commands.name: /claude-api
commands.summary: Loads Claude API reference material for the project language (Python, TypeScript, Java, Go, Ruby, C#, PHP, cURL) as well as Managed Agents reference.
commands.what:
Loads Claude API reference material for the project language (Python, TypeScript, Java, Go, Ruby, C#, PHP, cURL) as well as Managed Agents reference.

The 'migrate' subcommand updates existing API code to a newer model (model IDs, thinking configuration, etc.). The 'managed-agents-onboard' subcommand walks interactively through creating a new Managed Agent.

whenGood.title: Load reference material before writing your own code against the Claude API
whenGood.example: /claude-api — before building a custom streaming handler for the Messages API

whenGood.title: Migrate existing API code to a newer model
whenGood.example: /claude-api migrate — update model IDs and thinking configuration in existing code

whenBad.why: /claude-api loads API reference material (Python/TS/Java/...), not CLI documentation
whenBad.alternative: use the claude-code-guide agent or the official Claude Code docs for questions about the CLI itself

commands.what:

commands.name: /compact
commands.summary: Summarizes the conversation so far to free up context.
commands.what:
Summarizes the conversation so far to free up space in the context window. Optionally you pass a focus instruction as an argument, for example /compact focus on open TODOs and next steps — the summary then specifically keeps what you specify, instead of what the automatic pass considers important.

Project CLAUDE.md and auto-memory are then automatically reloaded from disk; path-bound rules and nested CLAUDE.md files in subfolders, on the other hand, are lost until the corresponding file is read again. Invoked skill content is also reloaded, but capped at 5,000 tokens per skill and 25,000 tokens in total.

whenGood.title: Free up context while continuing work on the same topic
whenGood.example: /compact

whenGood.title: Steer the summary specifically
whenGood.example: /compact focus on open TODOs and next steps

whenBad.title: Complete change of topic
whenBad.why: /compact summarizes the conversation so far and keeps the thread; for a complete change of topic, this drags along unnecessary baggage according to the docs — the docs explicitly name /clear as the way for unrelated new work.
whenBad.alternative: /clear

commands.name: /cost
commands.summary: Alias for /usage.
commands.what:
`/cost` is, according to the reference table, literally an "Alias for /usage". When you call `/cost`, the same view opens as with `/usage`: the session block at the top shows the token usage of the current session, which Claude Code calculates locally from token counts at list prices — without promotional pricing or contract discounts. For binding billing, the doc points to the usage page in the Claude Console.

On Pro, Max, Team, or Enterprise plans, the view additionally shows plan usage limits, activity statistics, and a breakdown by skill, subagent, plugin, and MCP server. Since version 2.1.211, these totals reset to $0 on every `/clear`; before that, they kept accumulating over the entire process runtime.

Besides `/cost`, there is a second alias, `/stats`, which jumps directly to the stats tab of the same view.

whenGood.title: Check costs quickly
whenGood.example: Type `/cost` without having to remember the actual command name `/usage`.

whenGood.title: Compare usage against the plan limit
whenGood.example: As a Pro or Max subscriber, call `/cost` to see plan usage limits and activity statistics at a glance.

whenBad.title: Expecting standalone functionality
whenBad.why: According to the doc, the command is just an alias, not a separate command with different behavior.
whenBad.alternative: Use `/usage` directly, or `/stats` for the stats tab of the same view.

whenBad.title: Wanting to read binding billing figures
whenBad.why: The dollar amount shown is calculated locally from token counts at list prices and can differ from the actual invoiced amount.
whenBad.alternative: For binding billing, open the usage page in the Claude Console.

commands.name: /design-login
commands.summary: Authorizes access to the design system for /design-sync via the claude.ai account.
commands.what:
`/design-login` authorizes access to your design system for `/design-sync` via your claude.ai account. The command itself doesn't sync anything — it only establishes the account connection that `/design-sync` needs afterward.

`/design-sync [hint]` converts your repo's React design system and uploads it to Claude Design so designs generated by Claude use your real components; optionally you name the design system in the process, e.g. `/design-sync Acme DS`. An initial sync verifies every component and can take several hours for a large repo.

Important for availability: `/design-sync` only runs via the Anthropic API. On Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform, Microsoft Foundry, and Claude Platform on AWS, the underlying tool can't reach claude.ai — both commands are unavailable there.

whenGood.title: Authorize before the first design sync
whenGood.example: Run `/design-login` before syncing your own React design system for the first time.

whenGood.title: Reconnect after switching accounts
whenGood.example: Call `/design-login` again if `/design-sync` suddenly loses access to the design system.

whenBad.title: Expecting an immediate sync
whenBad.why: The command only authorizes access via the claude.ai account, it doesn't sync anything itself.
whenBad.alternative: Then run `/design-sync` for the actual sync.

whenBad.title: On Bedrock, Vertex, or Foundry
whenBad.why: According to the doc, `/design-sync` is unavailable on Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform, Microsoft Foundry, and Claude Platform on AWS — the authorization then goes nowhere.
whenBad.alternative: Switch to the direct Anthropic API if design sync is needed.

commands.name: /effort
commands.summary: Sets the model's effort level (reasoning depth).
commands.what:
`/effort` controls how much adaptive reasoning the model applies to each step. Depending on the model, `low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh`, `max`, and `ultracode` are available; `max` and `ultracode` only apply to the current session. `auto` resets to the model default. Without an argument, `/effort` opens an interactive slider; with an argument, the change takes effect immediately, without waiting for the current response to finish.

`ultracode` isn't a real model effort level but a Claude Code setting: it sends `xhigh` to the model and additionally lets Claude orchestrate dynamic workflows for larger tasks.

Since version 2.1.205, `/effort` with a level argument also works in non-interactive mode (`-p`), but then only for the current session. For some models, Claude Code initially holds their default effort level; as long as this hold is active, a non-interactive `/effort` reports "Not applied" — in that case, only `--effort` at startup helps.

whenGood.title: Increase reasoning effort before a tricky task
whenGood.example: /effort high

whenGood.title: Choose a level interactively via slider
whenGood.example: /effort

whenBad.title: A fundamentally different model is needed
whenBad.why: /effort only changes the reasoning effort level of the current model, not the model's capabilities.
whenBad.alternative: /model

whenBad.title: Changing it non-interactively while a model default hold is active
whenBad.why: For some models, Claude Code holds their default effort level in place the first time they're used; as long as this hold is active, a non-interactive /effort (-p) simply reports 'Not applied'.
whenBad.alternative: Pass --effort when starting Claude Code instead of setting /effort during a running -p call.

commands.name: /exit
commands.summary: Exits the CLI.
commands.what:
Exits the CLI, which also ends all background tasks running in the session, such as Bash processes or monitors — they're automatically cleaned up on exit, not continued.

In an attached background session (see /background), /exit behaves differently: here the command only disconnects from the terminal, the session itself keeps running in the background. You can reattach via claude agents, or — if the session has finished in the meantime — via the /resume picker, where background sessions appear marked with bg. If you actually want to stop such a session instead of just detaching, use /stop while you're still attached. Alias: /quit.

whenGood.title: Cleanly exit a session once the task is done
whenGood.example: /exit after finishing the work

whenGood.title: Deliberately only detach from a background session

whenBad.title: You actually want to stop an attached background session
whenBad.why: According to the docs, /exit only disconnects in an attached background session, the session keeps running.
whenBad.alternative: use /stop while still attached

whenBad.title: Running background Bash processes or monitors should keep running
whenBad.why: According to the docs, background tasks are automatically cleaned up on exit instead of continued — only backgrounding the session hands them off to a session that keeps running.
whenBad.alternative: use /background instead of /exit to keep the session running in the background along with its running tasks

commands.name: /export
commands.summary: Exports the current conversation as plain text.
commands.what:
/export opens a menu where you either copy the current conversation to the clipboard or save it as a plain text file. Messages and tool outputs are rendered as readable text — meant for a human to read, not as raw data or a structured format.

If you pass a filename directly, e.g. /export session-notes.txt, the command skips the menu and writes straight to that file. Without an argument, you get the choice between clipboard and file.

If you instead want to process the conversation programmatically, /export isn't the right tool according to the docs: for structured data for scripting, there are other paths, such as a non-interactive run with JSON output or accessing the session's locally stored transcript file.

whenGood.example: Call /export without an argument and choose the clipboard option in the dialog.

whenBad.why: According to the docs, /export produces a human-readable text format, not structured data for scripts.
whenBad.alternative: Use claude -p with --output-format json or stream-json to get the result, session ID, and cost in machine-readable form.

whenBad.title: Only wanting to copy the last response
whenBad.why: /export exports the entire conversation, not a single response.
whenBad.alternative: Use /copy to copy only the last (or, with a number, the n-th-to-last) response.

commands.name: /fast
commands.summary: Turns Fast mode on or off.
commands.what:
Turns Fast mode on or off.

/feedback opens the dialog for sending product feedback about Claude Code itself — not about your own project code. You first choose how much session history to include: just the current session, or additionally other sessions from the same project from the last 24 hours or 7 days. /bug and its alias /share open the same dialog; all three send via the same path. If you're signed in directly with Anthropic, the report goes to Anthropic and transcripts are retained for 5 years; via a third-party provider or without Anthropic credentials, the report instead lands locally under ~/.claude/feedback-bundles/ and has to be forwarded yourself. The environment variable DISABLE_FEEDBACK_COMMAND=1 can disable sending entirely.

whenGood.example: Call /feedback and include the last 24 hours of the same project instead of just the current session.

whenBad.title: Wanting to report a bug in your own project code
whenBad.why: According to the docs, /feedback addresses problems with Claude Code itself, not with your own application.
whenBad.alternative: Write a normal bug-fix prompt or open an issue in your own repo.

commands.what:
/help shows an overview of help and all available commands directly in the terminal. In the official command reference, it's documented with only this one sentence and isn't marked as either a skill or a workflow, but is built directly into the CLI — so it works the same regardless of plan and platform.

As an alternative, you can also just type /: this also opens a command list to browse, and if you then type more letters, Claude Code filters the list live to match command names. /help is thus best suited for initial orientation or looking up the full list, while / plus letters is better suited for quickly finding a command name you already vaguely remember.

whenGood.title: Look up a forgotten command name
whenGood.example: Call /help to look up a vaguely remembered command name in the full overview.

whenBad.title: Filtering specifically for a known command
whenBad.why: According to the docs, /help only shows the general overview; typing right after the slash filters the list live and is therefore more targeted.

whenBad.why: According to the docs, /help only provides a brief overview of commands, not a detailed explanation of individual features.
whenBad.alternative: Consult the official docs at code.claude.com/docs or ask specifically.

commands.what: Shows hook configurations for tool events.

commands.name: /ide
commands.summary: Manages IDE integrations and shows their status.
commands.what:
/ide manages the connection between Claude Code and your editor and shows its status. From an external terminal — that is, not the IDE's own integrated terminal — the command establishes the connection to a detected VS Code or JetBrains IDE (such as IntelliJ IDEA, PyCharm, WebStorm) and activates features like diff view in the editor, shared selection context, and automatically shared diagnostic messages.

If a supported IDE is running but doesn't yet have the matching plugin installed, /ide installs it automatically and then asks you to restart the IDE; once connected successfully, Claude Code confirms this with a message like "Connected to IntelliJ IDEA.". If, on the other hand, you start claude directly from your IDE's integrated terminal, Claude Code usually connects automatically without you having to run /ide manually.

whenGood.title: Establish the connection from an external terminal
whenGood.example: Start claude from a regular terminal (not the IDE terminal) and run /ide there to connect to a running VS Code or JetBrains IDE

whenGood.title: Check the IDE connection status
whenGood.example: After opening VS Code alongside the terminal, run /ide to confirm that Claude Code is connected

whenBad.title: Wanting to install the IDE extension for the first time
whenBad.why: /ide only automatically installs the plugin when it detects a running but not-yet-connected IDE — without a running IDE, the command isn't enough for the initial install.
whenBad.alternative: Install the matching Claude Code extension directly from the editor's marketplace (VS Code Marketplace or JetBrains Marketplace)

whenBad.title: Claude is already running in the integrated IDE terminal
whenBad.why: In this case, Claude Code usually connects automatically; /ide is then mostly unnecessary.

whenGood.title: Spot recurring friction points in your workflow

commands.name: /keybindings
commands.summary: Opens the keybindings file.
commands.what:
`/keybindings` opens your keyboard shortcut configuration file at `~/.claude/keybindings.json` — if it doesn't exist yet, it's created. The file is a JSON object with a `bindings` array: each block defines a context (e.g. `Global`, `Chat`, `Settings`, `Transcript`) and, within it, a mapping of key combinations to actions in the format `namespace:action`, such as `chat:submit` for sending a message or `app:toggleTodos` for showing/hiding the to-do list.

You can disable default shortcuts with `null`, combine multiple modifiers (`ctrl+shift+c`), and define key sequences (chords) like `ctrl+k ctrl+s`. Changes to the file are detected automatically and applied immediately — no restart is needed. Some combinations like Ctrl+C, Ctrl+D, or Ctrl+M are reserved and can't be reassigned. When loading, Claude Code checks the file for parse errors, invalid contexts, and reserved or duplicate bindings, and writes warnings to the debug log (start with `--debug` for details).

whenGood.title: Shortcut conflicts with another app
whenGood.example: Open /keybindings and, for example, reassign the default shortcut for `chat:externalEditor` to a different combination if that shortcut is already taken by the terminal or tmux.

whenGood.title: Create your own chord combination
whenGood.example: Add an entry like "ctrl+k ctrl+s": "chat:stash" in the `Chat` context of the file to define your own key sequence.

whenBad.title: Just quickly check which shortcuts currently exist, without changing anything
whenBad.why: /keybindings opens the editable file directly instead of a pure overview of the default configuration.
whenBad.alternative: Consult the tables in the docs about keyboard shortcuts instead of opening the file.

whenBad.title: Remap Vim mode keys like 'jj' to Escape
whenBad.why: According to the docs, Vim keys themselves can't be remapped via the keybindings file.
whenBad.alternative: Use the `vimInsertModeRemaps` setting to map INSERT mode key sequences.

commands.name: /login
commands.summary: Signs in to your Anthropic account.
commands.what:
`/login` starts the sign-in process for your Anthropic account. On the very first start of Claude Code, a browser window opens automatically for this; after that, you can call `/login` manually at any time, for example to sign in again after a `/logout` or to switch accounts. Supported are Claude Pro/Max, Claude for Teams/Enterprise, the Claude Console, cloud providers such as Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform, or Microsoft Foundry (via environment variables or the "3rd-party platform" option in the login prompt), as well as a self-hosted Claude Apps Gateway via enterprise SSO.

If the browser doesn't open automatically, press `c` to copy the login URL to the clipboard. If the browser shows a code instead — common with WSL2, SSH sessions, or containers — paste it directly into the terminal. Once complete, the terminal reports "Login successful". If an existing login expires in less than three days, Claude Code warns you on startup and recommends `/login` to renew it.

whenGood.title: First sign-in on a new machine
whenGood.example: After installation, start `claude` in the terminal and run /login to connect to your Claude account via browser.

whenGood.title: Renew an expiring login
whenGood.example: When you see the message 'Your login expires in 3 days · run /login to renew', simply run /login to extend the login without interrupting the current session.

whenBad.title: Just wanting to check the current login status
whenBad.why: /login starts a new login flow directly instead of just displaying information.
whenBad.alternative: Use /status — among other things, it shows a login line with account and expiration status.

whenBad.title: Work via API key or your own credential script
whenBad.why: ANTHROPIC_API_KEY, ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN, or apiKeyHelper operate independently of the /login flow and take precedence over subscription login in the auth order.
whenBad.alternative: Set the appropriate environment variable or configure apiKeyHelper instead of logging in via /login.

commands.name: /logout
commands.summary: Signs out of your Anthropic account.
commands.what:
`/logout` signs you out of the currently connected Anthropic account. The command removes the stored credentials (`.credentials.json`, depending on the operating system in the macOS keychain, at `~/.claude/.credentials.json` on Linux, or at `%USERPROFILE%\.claude\.credentials.json` on Windows) and additionally resets the first-launch setup state: if you start Claude Code again afterward with `claude`, it walks you through login and initial setup completely again.

Use `/logout` to sign in again — for example with a different account or after switching organizations — or to cleanly disconnect an account from a shared machine. The command only affects the login stored via `/login`; credentials via `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`, `ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN`, or `apiKeyHelper` run as separate credential paths independently of it.

whenGood.title: Disconnect an account on a shared machine
whenGood.example: After working on a team/test machine, run /logout so the next person has to sign in with their own account.

whenGood.title: Switch to a different account or organization
whenGood.example: Run /logout and then /login to reconnect with a different Claude account.

whenBad.title: Just briefly checking which account is currently active
whenBad.why: /logout ends the login immediately instead of just displaying information.
whenBad.alternative: Use /status to view the login line with account and expiration info without signing out.

whenBad.title: Wanting to end a login via ANTHROPIC_API_KEY or apiKeyHelper
whenBad.why: According to the docs, /logout only manages the .credentials.json login stored via /login; API key- or helper-based access runs via environment variables or configuration.
whenBad.alternative: Remove the environment variable (e.g. ANTHROPIC_API_KEY) in the terminal or adjust the apiKeyHelper setting in the config.

commands.name: /powerup
commands.summary: Shows Claude Code features through short interactive lessons with animated demos.
commands.what:
`/powerup` introduces you to Claude Code features through short, interactive lessons with animated demos — right in the terminal, without having to separately open the docs.

The command was introduced in version 2.1.90 and is aimed at anyone who wants to try out new or little-used features rather than just read about them: each lesson shows a feature via an animated demo, so you can see directly how it behaves in practice.

`/powerup` isn't meant as a pure lookup reference for all commands — `/help` provides that overview, and the official docs at code.claude.com provide the details. `/powerup` is more of a playful way to get to know Claude Code better step by step, rather than a reference work for targeted questions.

commands.name: /privacy-settings
commands.summary: Shows and changes your privacy settings.
commands.what:
/privacy-settings opens your privacy settings for editing directly from within Claude Code. According to the docs, the command is only visible to Pro and Max plan subscribers — not on the free plan.

The content is mainly about consent for whether your data may be used to train future Claude models. This setting also affects the retention period: with consent enabled, Anthropic stores your data for 5 years; with it disabled, only for 30 days. The same setting can alternatively also be changed directly in the browser at claude.ai/settings/data-privacy-controls.

For Team, Enterprise, and API users, separate, contractually regulated privacy terms apply anyway (Commercial Terms, optionally Zero Data Retention), which is why no personal toggle is provided for them via this command.

whenGood.example: Open /privacy-settings and check whether the use of your own data for model training is enabled.

whenBad.alternative: Ask your organization admin about the applicable Commercial Terms or Zero Data Retention.

If no browser is available — for example in a pure SSH session or a container without a graphical interface — Claude Code instead prints the stream URL as text in the terminal, which you can open manually in any player. According to the docs, the command is not available on Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform, Microsoft Foundry, and Claude Platform on AWS. According to Anthropic's weekly recap (Week 27, June 29 – July 3, 2026), `/radio` was newly added with releases v2.1.195–v2.1.201.

commands.name: /rewind
commands.summary: Resets the conversation and/or the code to an earlier point, or summarizes from a selected message onward.
commands.what:
`/rewind` opens a menu with every prompt you've sent in the session. You choose a point and then an action: restore code and conversation, restore only the conversation, restore only the code, summarize from here, or summarize up to this point. The two code options only appear if there are actually tracked file changes at that point.

Instead of the command, you can also press `Esc` twice on an empty input line to open the same menu. Since version 2.1.191, you can even rewind past a cleared conversation: after `/clear`, an additional entry appears in the menu to return to the previous session.

Summarizing doesn't change any files — it only compresses part of the conversation history into a summary; the original messages remain in the transcript.

Aliases: `/checkpoint`, `/undo`.

commands.name: /scroll-speed
commands.summary: Interactively adjusts the mouse wheel scroll speed.
commands.what:
/scroll-speed interactively adjusts the mouse wheel scroll speed. The command is only available in fullscreen rendering — an optional, experimental display mode that you activate beforehand via /tui fullscreen — and not there in the JetBrains IDE terminal.

The dialog shows a ruler that you scroll while the window is open, to feel the change immediately. With ← / → you set the speed in whole steps up to 10, and on terminals with finer control additionally in quarter steps from 0.25. r resets to the automatically detected default value, Enter saves. The saved value corresponds to the environment variable CLAUDE_CODE_SCROLL_SPEED and ends up permanently in ~/.claude/settings.json; values higher than 10 can only be set via the variable. Regardless of the base speed, Claude Code automatically accelerates fast scrolling — this can be turned off via wheelScrollAccelerationEnabled: false in the settings.

whenGood.title: Permanently adjust the scroll speed
whenGood.example: open /scroll-speed in the fullscreen terminal, set it to the desired speed with ←/→, and save with Enter — the value ends up in ~/.claude/settings.json.

whenGood.example: open /scroll-speed and press r to correct a speed set too high or too low.

whenBad.alternative: activate /tui fullscreen first; in the JetBrains terminal use the IDE's own scroll settings instead (from JetBrains 2025.3 also with automatic fixes from Claude Code for known scroll bugs)

whenBad.title: The terminal doesn't forward mouse wheel events
whenBad.why: According to the docs, the live preview in the ruler only responds to mouse wheel events that the terminal forwards to Claude Code — iTerm2, for example, blocks this by default via a profile setting.
whenBad.alternative: In iTerm2, enable 'Enable mouse reporting' under Settings → Profiles → Terminal, then open /scroll-speed again

commands.name: /setup-bedrock
commands.summary: Configures Amazon Bedrock authentication, region, and model pins via an interactive wizard.
commands.what:
/setup-bedrock opens an interactive wizard that sets up sign-in to Amazon Bedrock: it asks for the authentication method (a detected AWS profile, an Amazon Bedrock API key, access key/secret, or already-set environment variables), takes over your AWS region, and checks which Claude models your account is allowed to call so you can save them as fixed model pins. When run again, model selection starts from your currently pinned models. The wizard writes the result into the `env` block of your settings.json (`~/.claude/settings.json` or `$CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR/settings.json`) — so you no longer have to export environment variables by hand.

The command only appears in the command menu once Bedrock is configured, but it already works if you type it beforehand, as long as `CLAUDE_CODE_USE_BEDROCK=1` is set. First-time users can alternatively reach the same wizard directly via the login screen.

whenGood.title: Team switches to Amazon Bedrock
whenGood.example: With `CLAUDE_CODE_USE_BEDROCK=1` set, run `/setup-bedrock` to interactively set up authentication, region, and model pins

whenGood.title: Change credentials or model pins later
whenGood.example: Call `/setup-bedrock` again to update credentials, region, or pinned model versions — the selection starts from the existing pins

whenBad.title: Without the env var set, or with normal Anthropic usage
whenBad.why: /setup-bedrock is meant for Amazon Bedrock sign-in and only appears in the menu once CLAUDE_CODE_USE_BEDROCK=1 is set; direct Anthropic account usage doesn't need the command.
whenBad.alternative: First set CLAUDE_CODE_USE_BEDROCK=1, or simply use /login for direct Anthropic API usage

commands.name: /setup-vertex
commands.summary: Configures authentication, project, region, and model pins for Google Cloud's Agent Platform.
commands.what:
`/setup-vertex` configures authentication, project, region, and model pins for Google Cloud's Agent Platform (the docs now call the former "Vertex AI" this way, though the login screen still shows "Google Vertex AI") via an interactive wizard.

`/setup-vertex` is only visible as a standalone slash command when `CLAUDE_CODE_USE_VERTEX=1` is set. Without this variable, you can still reach the same wizard: on the first start of `claude`, choose "3rd-party platform" and then "Google Vertex AI" at the login prompt — if you're already logged in, `/login` opens the same menu.

Once you've gone through the wizard, you can call `/setup-vertex` again at any time afterward to change credentials, project, region, or model pins; the model pin step then starts from your currently pinned models. The result is saved in `~/.claude/settings.json`, or in `$CLAUDE_CONFIG_DIR/settings.json` if that variable is set.

whenGood.title: Team uses Google Cloud's Agent Platform
whenGood.example: With CLAUDE_CODE_USE_VERTEX=1 set, run /setup-vertex to set up authentication, project, region, and model pins via the wizard.

whenGood.title: Adjust model pins later

commands.name: /stats
commands.summary: Alias for /usage, opens directly to the Stats tab.
commands.what:
`/stats` is an alias for `/usage` and opens the view directly on the Stats tab. `/usage` itself shows session costs, your plan's usage limits, and activity statistics; at the top is a session block with token consumption and costs calculated locally from token counts at list prices. This block is aimed primarily at API users, since subscription users (Pro/Max/Team/Enterprise) have their quota included in the plan and instead see usage bars, activity statistics, and a usage breakdown. On Pro, Max, Team, and Enterprise plans, the breakdown attributes recent usage to skills, subagents, plugins, and individual MCP servers; `d`/`w` switches between the last 24 hours and the last 7 days.

According to the changelog, `/stats` and `/cost` were historically standalone commands that were merged into `/usage` — both continue to exist as keyboard shortcuts that open the respective tab directly.

whenGood.title: Quick cost/usage check while working
whenGood.example: Type /stats to immediately see session costs and token consumption in the Stats tab of /usage.

whenGood.title: Check how close you are to plan limits
whenGood.example: As a Pro or Max user, run /stats to view the usage bars and the breakdown by skills/subagents/MCP servers for the last 24 hours or 7 days.

whenBad.title: Referencing /stats as a standalone command with its own function in docs or scripts
whenBad.why: According to the docs, /stats is just an alias for /usage that opens the Stats tab directly — it has no standalone functionality.
whenBad.alternative: Reference /usage, which represents the full command and feature set.

whenBad.title: Needing authoritative billing data for the organization
whenBad.why: The costs shown in /usage or /stats are calculated locally from token counts at list prices and can differ from the actual invoice.
whenBad.alternative: Use the usage page in the Claude Console (platform.claude.com/usage) for authoritative billing data.

commands.name: /status
commands.summary: Opens the settings interface to the Status tab with version, model, account, and connectivity.
commands.what:
/status opens the settings UI directly on the status tab and shows you at a glance the installed Claude Code version, the model currently in use, the signed-in account, and the connection status to Anthropic. This is handy for quick debugging: if Claude behaves unexpectedly, seems to be using the wrong model, or there are connection issues, you can see the current state here immediately. On Amazon Bedrock, /status additionally shows where the AWS region being used comes from.

Unlike most commands, /status — like /tasks and /usage — runs immediately without interrupting the current response: you can type it even in the middle of a Claude turn, without having to wait for Claude to finish answering.

whenGood.title: Check version/model/account/connection
whenGood.example: Call /status to see which Claude Code version, which model, and which account are currently active, e.g. when debugging unexpected behavior

whenGood.title: Query status in the middle of a running response
whenGood.example: While Claude is still answering, type /status to check the version or connectivity, without interrupting or waiting for the running response

whenBad.title: Looking for token/cost info
whenBad.why: /status shows version, model, account, and connectivity, but no usage or cost data.
whenBad.alternative: Use /usage (aliases: /cost, /stats)

commands.summary: Configures Claude Code's status line.
commands.what:
Configures Claude Code's status line.

Describe what you want, or leave it without an argument for auto-configuration from the shell prompt.

commands.name: /stickers
commands.summary: Orders Claude Code stickers.
commands.what:
`/stickers` is a simple, standalone command with no arguments from the "All commands" reference table. The doc describes it literally in one sentence: "Order Claude Code stickers" — invoked in the running chat, it starts the ordering process for physical Claude Code stickers.

Neither flags nor optional arguments are documented, and the reference doesn't mention any plan- or platform-specific restriction for `/stickers` itself. However, the doc's general note applies to all commands in principle: not every command appears for every user, depending on platform, plan, and environment — as an example, the doc explicitly names `/upgrade`, which isn't shown on Enterprise plans.

The command is marked neither as a skill nor as a workflow, so it belongs to the built-in commands: its behavior is hardcoded in the CLI, not in a prompt to Claude.

whenGood.title: Order stickers for the team
whenGood.example: Call `/stickers` to order Claude Code stickers for yourself or your team.

whenGood.title: Get stickers for a meetup
whenGood.example: Before a local dev meetup, type `/stickers` to order stickers to hand out to attendees.

whenBad.title: Expecting productive use
whenBad.why: According to the doc, the command only has the function "Order Claude Code stickers" — no connection to actual development work.
whenBad.alternative: For productive tasks, use one of the development commands like `/code-review` or `/plan`.

commands.name: /tasks
commands.summary: Lists background tasks of the current session and attached background sessions.
commands.what: Lists background tasks of the current session and attached background sessions.

commands.name: /upgrade
commands.summary: Opens the upgrade page in your browser to switch to a higher plan tier.
commands.what:
`/upgrade` opens the upgrade page in your browser so you can switch to a higher plan tier — so it's about your subscription, not the installed software. If the browser fails to open automatically, the command shows a sign-in prompt instead, according to the doc, without printing the URL itself.

The command's visibility depends on plan and platform: the official reference explicitly states that `/upgrade` isn't shown on Enterprise plans. According to the changelog, it was introduced to simplify switching to Claude Max plans.

`/upgrade` isn't responsible for updating the installed Claude Code version. `/doctor` instead points to a newer version in the release channel during the setup check; the update itself runs via the regular installation path or your package manager.

whenGood.title: Switch to a higher plan tier
whenGood.example: Call `/upgrade` to open the upgrade page in the browser and, for example, switch from Pro to Max.

whenGood.title: Get more capacity after hitting a limit
whenGood.example: After a limit notification, type `/upgrade` to switch directly to a higher plan tier instead of waiting for the reset.

whenBad.title: Expecting a CLI update
whenBad.why: According to the doc, the command switches the plan tier and opens the browser upgrade page for that — it doesn't update the installed Claude Code version.
whenBad.alternative: Update the version via the regular installation path or package manager; `/doctor` points to a newer version.

whenBad.title: Use on an Enterprise plan
whenBad.why: The official reference explicitly states that `/upgrade` isn't shown on Enterprise plans.
whenBad.alternative: Clarify plan changes with the responsible admin or team/enterprise management.

commands.name: /usage
commands.summary: Also shows plan limits and activity stats, not just API costs
commands.what:
`/usage` shows you how much you've used in the current session: token counts, an estimated cost figure, and — on Pro, Max, Team, and Enterprise plans — your plan limits and activity stats.

Claude Code calculates the cost figure in the session block locally from the token counts at standard list prices; it can therefore differ from your actual bill and is mainly relevant for API users. On a subscription plan, `/usage` additionally shows a breakdown of what counts against your limit — by skill, subagent, plugin, and individual MCP servers, plus notes on cost drivers like long context or cache misses at a 10% share or higher. Use `d`/`w` to switch between the last 24 hours and the last 7 days. The numbers come only from the local session history on this device — other devices or claude.ai are not included.

Aliases: `/cost` and `/stats` (the latter opens directly to the stats tab).

whenGood.title: Regular cost overview
whenGood.example: Call /usage to keep an eye on token counts, estimated costs, and — on subscription plans — plan limits before starting a bigger task.

whenGood.title: Find usage drivers by skill
whenGood.example: After a long /batch run, check /usage and use the breakdown by skill, subagent, plugin, and MCP server to see what consumed the largest share.

whenBad.title: Checking context window usage
whenBad.why: /usage shows token consumption, costs, and plan limits, but not how full the current context window is.
whenBad.alternative: use /context, which visualizes context usage as a colored grid.

whenBad.title: Needing a binding invoice total
whenBad.why: The dollar figure in the session block is calculated by Claude Code locally from token counts at standard list prices — this can differ from the actual invoice, since promotional pricing and discounts aren't factored in.
whenBad.alternative: For binding billing, use the usage page in the Claude Console.

commands.what:
Starts the project app and verifies that a change works end-to-end.

commands.name: /vim
commands.summary: No longer exists — removed in version 2.1.92.
commands.what:
`/vim` no longer exists. The command was removed from Claude Code in version 2.1.92 — along with `/tag`, which was dropped in the same version.

Since then, you toggle Vim mode via `/config` → Editor mode. The functionality itself hasn't changed: NORMAL, INSERT, and VISUAL modes along with their keyboard shortcuts still work exactly as before — only the dedicated slash command for it is gone. Handy detail: search in the `/config` menu also matches option values — type "vim" there and you jump directly to the matching editor mode setting instead of scrolling through the list manually.

On versions before 2.1.92, `/vim` still exists as a normal command.

whenGood.title: Quickly find the Vim setting

whenBad.title: On a version from 2.1.92 onward
whenBad.why: The command was removed in 2.1.92 and no longer does anything.
whenBad.alternative: use /config → Editor mode.

commands.name: /status
commands.summary: Shows the current status of the running Codex session.
commands.what: /status gives an overview of the running interactive session. It's part of the official list of Codex CLI slash commands used to check the state of the session instead of blindly changing settings like model or approval mode.

whenGood.title: Check which mode you're in before an important action
whenGood.example: /status — take a quick look before Codex is about to make changes to the repository

whenGood.title: Re-orient yourself after a longer break
whenGood.example: /status — get an overview when resuming work after an interruption

commands.name: /plan
commands.summary: Shows or manages the work plan for the current task.
commands.what: /plan is part of the official list of interactive Codex slash commands and refers to the plan for the task running within the session. It complements commands like /status and /goal, which let you track the goal and progress of a session.

whenGood.title: Overview of the planned steps before a larger task
whenGood.example: /plan — see how Codex intends to approach a multi-step task before approving it

whenGood.title: Check mid-task whether the plan still fits the task
whenGood.example: /plan — check during an ongoing implementation whether the next steps still make sense

whenBad.title: Task is trivial and single-step

commands.summary: Triggers a review of the current code changes.
commands.what: /review is part of the official list of Codex CLI's interactive slash commands. It lives in the same namespace as the CLI subcommand codex review, which can review changes with flags like --uncommitted, --base, --commit, or --title. Within a running session it lets you trigger a review of the changes made so far.

whenGood.title: Double-check your own changes before committing
whenGood.example: /review — have the current, not-yet-committed changes looked over

whenGood.title: Request a second look before a merge
whenGood.example: /review — have the session's changes checked before merging into the main branch

whenBad.why: /review requires a running interactive session.

commands.name: /diff
commands.summary: Shows the current changes (diff) of the session.
commands.what: /diff is part of the official list of interactive Codex slash commands and shows the changes Codex has made or proposed in the running session. It complements commands like /review, which additionally evaluate the changes.

whenGood.title: Quickly check what Codex has changed so far
whenGood.example: /diff — after a few work steps, check which files were affected

whenGood.title: See the exact line changes before approving
whenGood.example: /diff — look at the changes before letting Codex apply them

whenBad.title: You need a substantive assessment, not just the raw diff text
whenBad.why: /diff shows the changes but doesn't evaluate them.
whenBad.alternative: Use /review to additionally have the changes assessed

commands.name: /resume
commands.summary: Continues an earlier Codex session.
commands.what: /resume is part of the official list of interactive slash commands and matches the purpose of the CLI subcommand resume, which lets you continue sessions, including via resume --last or a specific session ID. Within the TUI, /resume lets you return to a previous session instead of starting fresh.

whenGood.title: Continue the same task after an interruption
whenGood.example: /resume — go back to the last session to keep working there

whenGood.title: Deliberately resume a specific earlier session
whenGood.example: /resume — pick the right one from a list of previous sessions

whenBad.title: You deliberately want to start completely fresh
whenBad.why: /resume picks up an existing session along with its context, which isn't wanted here.
whenBad.alternative: Use /new for a fresh session with no prior context

commands.name: /new
commands.summary: Starts a new, empty Codex session.
commands.what: /new is part of the official list of interactive Codex slash commands and starts a new session within the TUI. It's the opposite of /resume, which continues an existing session, and of /fork, which branches an existing session.

whenGood.title: Start a new, independent topic
whenGood.example: /new — start a fresh session for a task unrelated to the previous one

whenGood.title: Session is cluttered with old context
whenGood.example: /new — start over when the prior session history is no longer relevant

whenBad.title: The session's existing context is still needed
whenBad.why: /new discards the session's existing context.
whenBad.alternative: Use /resume to keep working on the existing session, or /fork to branch off a variant of it

commands.name: /fork
commands.summary: Branches the current session into a new, independent copy.
commands.what: /fork is part of the official list of interactive slash commands and serves the same purpose as the CLI subcommand of the same name, which belongs to session management alongside archive/unarchive/delete. It lets you use the session history so far as the starting point for a new, separate session.

whenGood.title: Try two different approaches from the same starting point
whenGood.example: /fork — branch off from the current session state to test an alternative approach without altering the original session

whenGood.title: Test a risky next step in isolation
whenGood.example: /fork — create a copy of the session before a larger change

whenBad.title: There should only be a single, linear session
whenBad.why: /fork creates an additional, separate session copy, which is unnecessary overhead here.
whenBad.alternative: Simply keep working in the existing session

commands.summary: Shows or manages the MCP servers connected to Codex.
commands.what: /mcp is part of the official list of interactive slash commands and corresponds to the CLI subcommands mcp and mcp-server, used to configure MCP servers. Within the session, /mcp gives access to the connected MCP servers.

whenGood.title: Check which MCP servers are currently available
whenGood.example: /mcp — see which external tools/servers are available to the session

whenGood.title: Verify access before a task that needs external tools
whenGood.example: /mcp — check whether a required MCP server is connected before starting a task that needs it

commands.name: /skills
commands.summary: Shows the skills available for the session.
commands.what: /skills is part of the official list of interactive Codex slash commands. It sits alongside /plugins in session controls; the exact details aren't further documented.

whenGood.title: Check available skills before a specialized task
whenGood.example: /skills — see which skills can be used for the upcoming task

whenGood.title: Get an overview when unsure what Codex can additionally do
whenGood.example: /skills — check the list before formulating a task that needs a special approach

whenBad.title: Task is trivial and needs no special skills
whenBad.why: For a simple change, checking available skills is an unnecessary extra step.

commands.name: /goal
commands.summary: Sets a persistent task goal that Codex works toward across the session.
commands.what: According to the official Codex CLI docs, /goal sets a persistent task goal. Unlike a one-off instruction, this goal persists across the session and guides Codex.

whenGood.title: Set an overarching goal for a longer work session
whenGood.example: /goal — e.g. set 'fix all open type errors in the project' as an ongoing goal

whenGood.title: Keep focus across multiple individual steps
whenGood.example: /goal — set a goal so Codex doesn't lose track across several consecutive instructions

commands.name: codex exec
commands.summary: Runs Codex non-interactively, e.g. for scripts or CI.
commands.what: codex exec (short form: e) runs a task non-interactively without opening the TUI. You can also pass '-' as the prompt to read input from stdin. With --json, events are output as JSONL; with -o/--output-last-message, only the last message is saved; and with --output-schema, an output schema is enforced.

whenGood.title: Integrate Codex into a script or pipeline
whenGood.example: codex exec "summarize the changes from the last commits" --json

whenGood.title: Pipe input from another source via stdin
whenGood.example: cat task.txt | codex exec -

whenBad.title: You want to steer interactively, e.g. answer follow-up questions live
whenBad.why: codex exec runs through without interactive follow-up questions.
whenBad.alternative: Start the normal TUI with codex (without exec)

commands.name: codex review
commands.summary: Runs a review of changes via the CLI.
commands.what:
codex review runs a code review non-interactively from the command line, i.e. without opening a running TUI session.

According to the docs, you choose exactly one review target: either `--uncommitted` (staged, unstaged, and untracked changes), `--base <branch>` (diff against a base branch), `--commit <SHA>` (changes from a specific commit), or your own review instructions as a free-text `PROMPT` (also readable from stdin with `-`) — according to the docs, these options are mutually exclusive. `--title` sets the displayed commit title in the review summary, but only works together with `--commit`. There's also `--strict-config`, which triggers an error if `config.toml` contains unknown fields. Distinct from the standalone `codex review` call is the slash command `/review`, which according to the Codex source code is used within an already-running interactive session and also accepts instructions as an inline argument there.

whenGood.title: Review uncommitted changes before committing
whenGood.example: codex review --uncommitted

whenGood.title: Review a specific commit with a title
whenGood.example: codex review --commit a1b2c3d --title "Fix login bug"

whenBad.title: Specifying multiple review targets at once
whenBad.why: According to the docs, --uncommitted, --base, --commit, and a custom PROMPT are mutually exclusive — only one option is allowed.
whenBad.alternative: choose exactly one target option, e.g. only --base main

whenBad.title: The review should be part of a running interactive session
whenBad.why: codex review is a standalone, non-interactive CLI call outside a running TUI session.
whenBad.alternative: use /review instead within a running session

commands.name: codex resume
commands.summary: Continues an earlier Codex session via the CLI.
commands.what:
codex resume continues a previous interactive session from the terminal, either specifically via a `SESSION_ID` or generally via `--last` for the most recently used session.

According to the docs, `--last` by default only refers to sessions in the current working directory; with `--all`, sessions outside the current directory are included too. `--include-non-interactive` additionally expands the selection (picker or `--last`) to include non-interactive sessions. The same resume logic exists for non-interactive mode as `codex exec resume [SESSION_ID]`, also with `--last`/`--all`, plus an optional directly appended follow-up `PROMPT` and `--image`/`-i` for attaching images to this follow-up task. Distinct from the standalone `codex resume` call is the slash command `/resume`, which according to the Codex source code is used within an already-running session to switch to a different saved session.

whenGood.title: Continue the last session directly
whenGood.example: codex resume --last

whenGood.title: Continue a session non-interactively in a script
whenGood.example: codex exec resume --last "briefly summarize the latest changes"

whenBad.title: Already in a running interactive session
whenBad.why: For switching within the TUI, the standalone CLI call codex resume is unnecessary.
whenBad.alternative: use /resume within the session

whenBad.title: Continuing a session from a different directory
whenBad.why: According to the docs, --last by default only refers to the current working directory.
whenBad.alternative: use codex resume --all to also include sessions outside the current directory

commands.name: /model

commands.what: /model opens the model picker (fuzzy search via [filter]) inside a running Cursor Agent session. Press Tab to edit the selected entry. Changes to Fast mode, reasoning effort, or context are preserved across a model switch. The model can also be set at startup with --model.

whenGood.title: Upgrade for a difficult task
