whenGood.title: Pick a faster model for routine work
whenGood.example: /model — switch to a cheaper model to, e.g., write commit messages

whenBad.title: The model should already be fixed at startup
whenBad.why: If you already know which model you need, there's no need to switch into the session and toggle it there.
whenBad.alternative: Set the model directly with a flag, e.g. agent --model opus

whenBad.title: Just jumping between known model families quickly
whenBad.why: The full fuzzy search of /model is more effort than needed for a quick jump to a known model.
whenBad.alternative: Use a model shortcut like /opus or /composer

commands.name: /run-everything
commands.summary: Toggles 'Run Everything' autopilot mode, which runs commands without asking for approval.
commands.what: /run-everything (alias /auto-run) toggles Run Everything on/off, or shows the current state with status. In this mode the agent runs commands without individual approval prompts.

whenGood.title: Many repetitive, low-risk steps in a row
whenGood.example: /run-everything on — e.g. for a long chain of lint fixes across many files

whenGood.title: Check the current autopilot state before a task
whenGood.example: /run-everything status — quick check before riskier steps come up

whenBad.title: Production or destructive commands are coming up
whenBad.why: Without prompts, the agent can accidentally delete data or change production systems.
whenBad.alternative: Use /sandbox or /auto-review instead for controlled approvals

whenBad.title: Only a single risky command needs to go through
whenBad.why: Turning on the full autopilot for that opens up more than needed.
whenBad.alternative: Just approve the single prompt normally instead of granting blanket approval

commands.name: /plan
commands.summary: Switches to Plan mode, where the agent drafts a plan before acting.
commands.what: /plan switches to Plan mode, shows the current plan, or submits a prompt directly in Plan mode. Plan mode has a persistent plan menu with 'Build Locally' and 'Build in Cloud' options; plans are saved to disk and can be transferred to cloud agents.

whenGood.title: Nail down the strategy before a bigger rework
whenGood.example: /plan Migrate the auth system to OAuth2 — review the plan before touching code

whenGood.title: Structure a multi-step task before the agent starts
whenGood.example: /plan — view and adjust the current plan before picking 'Build Locally'

whenBad.title: Just a short, unambiguous single change
whenBad.why: For a simple one-line change, going through a plan first is unnecessary.
whenBad.alternative: Prompt directly in the normal agent mode

whenBad.title: You just want to read and understand, not plan
whenBad.why: /plan targets execution planning, not pure research without intent to implement.
whenBad.alternative: Use /ask for read-only questions

commands.name: /ask
commands.summary: Toggles Ask mode, where the agent only reads and makes no changes.
commands.what: /ask toggles Ask mode for read-only questions. In Ask mode the agent can explore code and answer questions but cannot modify files or run commands with side effects. Also startable directly with --mode ask.

whenGood.title: Understand a codebase before planning changes
whenGood.example: /ask — then ask 'How is the auth middleware structured?'

whenGood.title: Make sure nothing gets changed by accident
whenGood.example: /ask — research in an unfamiliar repo with no write risk

whenBad.title: The agent actually needs to change code
whenBad.why: Changes are blocked in Ask mode, so the task doesn't move forward.
whenBad.alternative: Switch back to normal agent mode, or use /plan for structured implementation

whenBad.title: A multi-step plan needs to be produced
whenBad.why: /ask only gives answers, not step-by-step planning.
whenBad.alternative: Use /plan

commands.name: /debug
commands.summary: Toggles Debug mode, built for reproducing and narrowing down bugs.
commands.what: /debug toggles Debug mode, or submits a prompt directly in Debug mode. Reproduction-step cards are shown with their own (red) accent in Debug mode, so the active mode stays clear.

whenGood.title: Narrow down a specific bug
whenGood.example: /debug Login fails after a password reset

whenGood.title: Work through reproduction steps systematically
whenGood.example: /debug — activate the mode before pasting a bug report with a stack trace

whenBad.title: A new feature should be built directly
whenBad.why: Debug mode is built for bug-finding and narrowing, not new development.
whenBad.alternative: Use normal agent mode or /plan for feature work

whenBad.title: The bug is already clearly located
whenBad.why: If the cause and the fix are already clear, Debug mode adds no value.
whenBad.alternative: Ask for the fix directly in agent mode

commands.name: /logs
commands.summary: Shows the path to the current debug log file and copies it to the clipboard.
commands.what:
`/logs` is a slash command you enter within a running Cursor CLI session. It shows you the file path of the current session's debug log file and copies it to the clipboard at the same time.

Cursor continuously writes debug logs for every session. On shared machines, these logs have been stored separately per user since June 2026, so multiple accounts on the same host don't run into permission errors; the displayed path also stays visible on screen longer there.

So the command only gives you the path to the local log file — it neither shows the content nor uploads the file anywhere. For a specific support request, it makes sense to supplement it with `/copy-request-id`, which instead copies the ID of the last request, or `/about` for version and system info.

whenGood.title: Prepare a support request with the log file
whenGood.example: /logs — copy the path and attach it to a support ticket

whenGood.title: Find your own log path on a shared machine without permission errors
whenGood.example: Run /logs on a shared machine to get the user-specific log path

whenBad.title: You only need the last request ID, not the full log file
whenBad.why: /logs provides the file path, not a single ID.
whenBad.alternative: use /copy-request-id for the last request ID

whenBad.title: The log content should be shown directly in the terminal
whenBad.why: /logs only copies the path, but doesn't show the file's content.
whenBad.alternative: open the file at the copied path manually, e.g. with an editor

commands.name: /update
commands.summary: Updates Cursor Agent to the latest version directly from the running session.
commands.what: /update updates the CLI in place without leaving the session. The same thing also works via agent update in the terminal.

whenGood.title: Want to use a new feature from the changelog
whenGood.example: /update — then restart the session to load the new version

whenBad.title: In the middle of a critical, running task
whenBad.why: Updating mid-task can disturb the state of the current session.
whenBad.alternative: Push the update to after the task is done, or run agent update separately in the terminal

commands.name: /max-mode
commands.summary: Only available on old request-based pricing plans, not generally
commands.what:
/max-mode is a slash command from the official CLI reference and toggles "Max Mode" — according to the docs, explicitly only on old, request-based pricing plans ("legacy request-based plans"). Max Mode extends a model's context window beyond the default limit, which helps for tasks with unusually large amounts of context; but according to Cursor, the standard window is already enough for most coding tasks.

On current (non-legacy) pricing tiers, this toggle no longer exists on its own — there, models that need Max Mode activate it automatically themselves. On legacy plans, Max Mode is billed at the model's API price plus a 20% surcharge. The state appears as an indicator in the footer, and since July 2026 also in the prompt bar, and persists across sessions.

whenGood.title: Unlock more context for a large task on a legacy plan
whenGood.example: Enable /max-mode before running a model with a tight default context window on a very large repository

whenGood.title: Check whether Max Mode is currently active
whenGood.example: Call /max-mode and check the MAX indicator in the footer or prompt bar

whenBad.title: You're on a current (non-legacy) pricing plan
whenBad.why: According to the docs, Max Mode is only available as a toggle for users with an old, request-based subscription; it's absent on current plans.
whenBad.alternative: Use /model to directly select a model with a larger context window

whenBad.title: Routine, small coding task
whenBad.why: According to Cursor, the standard context window is enough for most tasks; Max Mode also costs a 20% surcharge on legacy plans.
whenBad.alternative: Work without Max Mode and only enable it when you actually need the context

commands.name: /rename
commands.summary: Renames the current chat session.
commands.what:
`/rename <name>` renames the current chat session of the Cursor CLI. You pass the desired name directly as an argument, e.g. `/rename Auth-Refactor`. The official slash command reference describes the command as "Rename the current chat session" — the doc doesn't mention further options.

According to the changelog entry from June 22, 2026, `/rename` belongs, together with `/copy`, to a series of improvements around input shortcuts, copying previous messages, and naming sessions.

A meaningful name mainly helps you find a session again later via `/resume` in the list of recent chats, instead of having to rely on timestamps.

whenGood.title: Make parallel sessions distinguishable
whenGood.example: Type `/rename Auth-Refactor` before switching between multiple open chats for different features.

whenGood.title: Mark a session for retrieval
whenGood.example: Before `/quit`, call `/rename Release-Prep` so the session stays recognizable via `/resume`.

whenBad.title: Just a short-lived session
whenBad.why: For a throwaway chat that's ending right afterward, renaming usually isn't worth it.
whenBad.alternative: Keep the default name and recognize the session by its content via `/resume` if needed.

commands.name: /clear
commands.summary: Starts a new, empty chat session.
commands.what:
`/clear` ends the current chat session and starts a new, empty session. The previous conversation history is no longer available as context within the new session afterward. `/new`, `/new-chat`, and `/newchat` are documented as equivalent aliases for the same command.

The command is useful for starting with a clean, empty context window on a topic change, for example when a task is finished and the next one has nothing to do with it. This keeps old context from unnecessarily affecting the response quality or token cost of the new task.

Importantly, `/clear` discards the history rather than compressing it. If you still need access to earlier messages, for example because you just want to free up space in the context window, `/summarize` (alias `/compress`) is the better choice, since it keeps a summary of the previous history. Old sessions can still be reopened later via `agent ls` or `/resume`.

whenGood.title: Free up the context window for a completely new topic
whenGood.example: /clear — after the previous task is finished

whenGood.title: Deliberately end an old session informally when you no longer need it
whenGood.example: /clear after finishing a task, when the session doesn't need to be referenced afterward

whenBad.title: The previous context is still needed
whenBad.why: /clear completely discards the current session's conversation history.
whenBad.alternative: Use /summarize to free up space without losing the context entirely

commands.name: /resume
commands.summary: Opens a list of recent chats across all workspaces and resumes one.
commands.what: /resume opens All chats across workspaces by default (Left/Right switches to 'This workspace'). Chats from other directories show a folder label; resuming one loads the full conversation instead of an empty session.

whenGood.title: Keep working on a task started yesterday
whenGood.example: /resume — pick yesterday's matching session from the list

whenGood.title: Find a chat from a different repo again
whenGood.example: /resume — filter by folder label to find the right workspace session

whenBad.title: Only the most recently used session needs to continue
whenBad.why: /resume first shows a picker list, an unnecessary step when it's clear which session is meant.
whenBad.alternative: Use --continue at startup (shorthand for --resume=-1)

whenBad.title: You want a completely new session
whenBad.why: /resume continues existing chats but doesn't start anything new.
whenBad.alternative: Use /clear

commands.name: /fork
commands.summary: Branches the current chat into a new session, the original stays untouched.
commands.what: /fork branches the current conversation into a copy and lets you pursue a different path in it. Aliases per the changelog: /branch, /duplicate.

whenGood.title: Try two different solution approaches in parallel
whenGood.example: /fork — then test an alternative implementation path in the new chat

whenGood.title: Hedge a risky attempt without endangering the main session
whenGood.example: /fork — branch off before an experimental refactor

whenBad.title: The existing path should just continue
whenBad.why: A fork creates an extra session you then have to manage, even though only linear continuation is needed.
whenBad.alternative: Keep writing normally in the current chat

whenBad.title: Old failed attempts should disappear entirely
whenBad.why: /fork keeps the original around, it doesn't clean anything up.
whenBad.alternative: Use /rewind to jump back to an earlier state

commands.name: /summarize
commands.summary: Summarizes the conversation to free up space in the context window.
commands.what: /summarize compresses the conversation so far to free up context. The command was renamed from /compress (to match the IDE); /compact and /compress still work as aliases.

whenGood.title: A long session is about to blow past the context window
whenGood.example: /summarize — after many turns, before the agent loses track

whenGood.title: Clean up before a topic switch within the same session
whenGood.example: /summarize — keep the key points, drop the detail noise

whenBad.title: Important detail must not be lost
whenBad.why: Summarizing loses the exact wording and detail fidelity of earlier messages.
whenBad.alternative: Write down important facts explicitly beforehand, or use /fork to keep a copy with the full history

whenBad.title: The context is still small
whenBad.why: Summarizing a short session barely saves space but still costs nuance.
whenBad.alternative: Just keep working normally

commands.name: /rewind
commands.summary: Jumps back to an earlier message via an interactive timeline and restores files/conversation.
commands.what: /rewind opens an interactive timeline to reset files and conversation state to an earlier turn, with a per-turn diff and the option to restore only the conversation (without files). On by default. Aliases per the changelog: /undo, /restore (must first be enabled in /config). Rewinding to an earlier turn also restores that turn's image attachments.

whenGood.title: A failed approach needs to be fully undone
whenGood.example: /rewind — jump back to the turn before the failed refactor

whenGood.title: Reset only the conversation state, but keep the files
whenGood.example: /rewind — choose the 'conversation-only restore' option

whenBad.title: Only a single typo needs correcting
whenBad.why: Jumping back through the whole timeline is overkill for a small correction.
whenBad.alternative: Just give a new correction instruction directly in the chat

whenBad.title: Two solution paths should be kept in parallel
whenBad.why: /rewind overwrites the later state instead of keeping it alongside.
whenBad.alternative: Use /fork beforehand to keep a copy

commands.name: /vim
commands.summary: Toggles Vim keybindings in the input field.
commands.what:
/vim is a slash command from the official CLI reference and toggles Vim keybindings in the prompt input field ("Toggle Vim keys"). According to the changelog, since May 2026 /vim can be triggered from any cursor position in the input field, not just when the prompt is empty. The active mode is shown in the footer.

The feature set grew step by step: search motions and operator combinations such as f/F/t/T/;/, (e.g. df, or ct.), a visual mode with delete and change operators, and individual character commands like r to replace a character. Ctrl+G additionally opens the current prompt in the external $EDITOR, letting you compose longer input there and then feed it back — handy in combination with /vim for anyone who prefers typing in their familiar editor.

whenGood.title: Use familiar Vim motions while writing long prompts
whenGood.example: Enable /vim, then navigate the input field with f/t search motions and operator combinations like df, or ct.

whenGood.title: Switch between insert and normal mode mid-prompt
whenGood.example: Type /vim at the current cursor position in the prompt, even when there's already text in the field

whenBad.title: You're more familiar with standard keybindings
whenBad.why: Vim keybindings change the behavior of familiar keys like i, dd, or Escape in the input field.
whenBad.alternative: Call /vim again to switch the mode back off

whenBad.title: You'd rather compose long prompts in your usual external editor
whenBad.why: Vim mode helps with editing inside the CLI input field itself, but doesn't replace a full-fledged editor.
whenBad.alternative: Use Ctrl+G to open the prompt in $EDITOR

commands.name: /line-numbers
commands.summary: Toggles line numbers in displayed code blocks.
commands.what:
`/line-numbers` toggles the display of line numbers in code blocks that the CLI shows in the chat history. The command doesn't need any arguments – calling it simply switches between on and off, for the current session.

With line numbers turned on, you can precisely point to a specific line when reading diffs or code excerpts, for example when you want to tell the agent which spot to change. This is especially helpful with longer files or functions, where a vague description like "the line with the condition" would be too imprecise. For very short snippets, however, the extra column tends to create visual noise rather than value, which is why the default state can differ depending on your working style.

whenGood.title: Point to specific lines
whenGood.example: /line-numbers — on, before saying 'check line 42'

whenGood.title: Prepare references before a pairing conversation
whenGood.example: /line-numbers on, before you discuss a function together in a call and want to name lines

whenBad.title: Only short code snippets without line references
whenBad.why: For short snippets, line numbers tend to get in the way rather than help.
whenBad.alternative: leave /line-numbers off for a more compact display

commands.name: /show-thinking
commands.summary: Toggles display of the model's thinking blocks.
commands.what:
`/show-thinking` is a simple toggle: the command shows or hides the model's internal thinking blocks in the running CLI session. According to the official reference table, the short description is simply "Toggle thinking block display" – the command takes no further arguments.

Thinking blocks show the internal intermediate-step text that some models generate before the actual answer. It's not documented whether the display starts on or off by default; the command merely toggles between the two states, based on the session's current state.

`/show-thinking` joins `/vim`, `/line-numbers`, and `/status-indicators` in the group of pure display toggles of the CLI – they only change the presentation in the terminal, not the model's behavior itself.

whenGood.title: Understand why the agent makes a certain decision
whenGood.example: /show-thinking on, before a complex architecture decision is coming up

whenGood.title: Read along the intermediate-step text when debugging unexpected agent behavior
whenGood.example: Turn on /show-thinking when a response seems hard to follow, and turn it off again afterward

whenBad.title: Only the final result matters, not the reasoning path
whenBad.why: Thinking blocks unnecessarily lengthen the visible output in the terminal when only the result counts.
whenBad.alternative: Leave /show-thinking off for a more compact session

commands.name: /status-indicators
commands.summary: Toggles status indicators in the terminal title.
commands.what:
`/status-indicators` toggles whether the CLI's current status is shown in the terminal window title. The command doesn't take any arguments, but switches between on and off with every call.

With the display turned on, you can tell from the terminal tab or window title that something is currently running in this session, without having to click into it first. This helps especially when several terminal windows or tabs are open in parallel and you want to see at a glance which session is still busy. If you already use the terminal title for something else, for example via your own prompt or status line script, the status display overwrites that text – in that case it's usually better to leave the command switched off.

whenGood.title: Recognize agent status even with a minimized terminal window
whenGood.example: /status-indicators — on, while a long task is running in the background

whenGood.title: Keep track of multiple terminal tabs in parallel
whenGood.example: /status-indicators on, when you're running agent sessions in several tabs at the same time

whenBad.title: The terminal title is used for something else, e.g. via a custom script
whenBad.why: The status display then overwrites your own title text.
whenBad.alternative: leave /status-indicators off

commands.name: /shell
commands.summary: Switches to Shell mode to run short commands directly without leaving the conversation.
commands.what: /shell switches to Shell mode for short commands within the session. Aliases: /sh, /run.

whenGood.title: Quickly check git status without leaving the chat context
whenGood.example: /shell git status

whenGood.title: Briefly inspect a file before the agent keeps working
whenGood.example: /sh ls -la src/

whenBad.title: The command should be part of a multi-step task planned by the agent
whenBad.why: /shell runs the command in isolation, without folding it into the agent's task planning.
whenBad.alternative: Phrase the command as a normal prompt instead, so the agent runs it in context

whenBad.title: You need persistent network/write access with clear limits
whenBad.why: /shell follows the normal session policy but offers no explicit path/network limits.
whenBad.alternative: Use agent sandbox run with --allow-paths/--network

commands.name: /about
commands.summary: Shows CLI version, system, and account info and copies it to the clipboard.
commands.what:
`/about` shows you the Cursor CLI version, system information, and account details within a running chat session. The command also automatically copies this info block to the clipboard, so you can reuse it without manually selecting it.

There's also an identically named terminal subcommand, `agent about`, which delivers the same info outside a chat session — according to the docs, though, without the automatic clipboard copy, which is only explicitly mentioned for the slash command `/about`.

A typical use case is preparing a bug report or support request: instead of looking up version, operating system, and account separately, you get the whole block with one command and paste it straight into the ticket. If you really only need the plain version number, the command gives you more information than necessary.

whenGood.title: Compile diagnostic info for a bug report
whenGood.example: /about — paste the output directly into the support ticket

whenGood.title: Quickly check which account and system you're currently working with
whenGood.example: Call /about to confirm account and system context before reporting a problem.

whenBad.title: You only need the plain version number
whenBad.why: /about delivers an entire info block, more than needed for a simple version check.
whenBad.alternative: Run agent --version in the terminal

commands.name: /setup-terminal
commands.summary: Configures terminal newline keybindings to match the detected terminal.
commands.what:
`/setup-terminal` detects your terminal program and sets up `Option+Enter` as a way to insert line breaks. According to the doc, iTerm2, Ghostty, Kitty, Warp, and Zed's integrated terminal already come with native support for `Shift+Enter` — the command isn't needed there. For Apple Terminal, Alacritty, and VS Code's integrated terminal, it handles the configuration.

In terminal multiplexers like tmux or screen, the command has no effect, because these intercept `Shift+Enter` themselves; there, according to the doc, `Ctrl+J` remains the most reliable alternative, working everywhere without configuration.

Those who prefer to set the keys themselves will find manual instructions in the doc — for example, sending `\x1b\r` for `Option+Enter`, with example configurations for iTerm2, Alacritty, and Kitty.

whenGood.title: Being able to write multi-line prompts
whenGood.example: After installing in Apple Terminal, run `/setup-terminal` once so `Option+Enter` inserts a line break instead of submitting.

whenGood.title: Set up the VS Code terminal
whenGood.example: Call `/setup-terminal` in the integrated VS Code terminal, because according to the doc it doesn't come with native `Shift+Enter` support.

whenBad.title: The terminal already supports Shift+Enter
whenBad.why: iTerm2, Ghostty, Kitty, Warp, and Zed's integrated terminal handle line breaks without setup, according to the doc.
whenBad.alternative: Simply use `Shift+Enter`.

whenBad.title: Working in tmux or screen
whenBad.why: Multiplexers intercept `Shift+Enter` themselves; according to the doc, the command has no effect there.
whenBad.alternative: Use `Ctrl+J` — according to the doc, the most reliable alternative.

commands.name: /help
commands.summary: Shows help; with a command name as an argument, shows details for that command.
commands.what:
`/help` shows an overview of all available slash commands in the Cursor CLI's chat prompt. If you call `/help <command>` with a command name as an argument, the CLI instead shows the details for exactly that command. The official reference describes this briefly as "Show help. Use /help <command> for command details."

The doc doesn't mention options beyond the optional argument. Invoking it doesn't change anything about code or session — it's purely for reference.

The slash command reference lists over 30 commands, from `/model` to `/bedrock` — `/help` is thus the central entry point for finding your way around this list without opening the docs website.

whenGood.title: Look up the syntax of a rarely used command
whenGood.example: Type `/help mcp` to see the exact syntax for MCP server management before using it.

whenGood.title: Get an overview of all commands
whenGood.example: Call `/help` without an argument to see the complete list of slash commands in the terminal.

whenBad.title: The command you're looking for is already well known
whenBad.why: The detour through help then only costs an extra step without providing new information.
whenBad.alternative: Call the command directly with the known arguments.

commands.name: /feedback
commands.summary: Sends feedback directly to the Cursor team.
commands.what:
`/feedback <message>` sends a message directly to the Cursor team, without you leaving the CLI or opening a separate form. You append your text directly to the command – for example a bug description, a request for a missing feature, or an observation about the behavior of another command.

Because the command expects a text argument according to the docs (`/feedback <message>`), calling it without an attached message doesn't produce usable feedback – only the text turns it into meaningful feedback. The channel is meant for short, targeted notes that arise directly in the context of your current session, not for detailed bug reports with attachments or for requests where you need a timely personal reply. For that, the docs point to dedicated support channels.

whenGood.title: Report a bug or missing feature
whenGood.example: /feedback /rewind sometimes jumps back two turns instead of one

whenGood.title: Give positive feedback about a workflow
whenGood.example: /feedback The new plan mode helped me a lot with a big refactor

whenBad.title: It's an urgent, individual support request
whenBad.why: Feedback messages aren't designed for quick 1:1 support.
whenBad.alternative: Use Cursor's official support channel

whenBad.title: Message is missing when calling the command
whenBad.why: /feedback <message> requires a text argument according to the reference table – without an attached message the command doesn't produce usable feedback.
whenBad.alternative: Always attach a short text directly, e.g. /feedback <your observation>

commands.name: /open
commands.summary: Opens the current repo's Git root directory in the Cursor editor.
commands.what:
`/open` opens the Git root directory of your current repository in Cursor, the editor. According to the docs, `/cursor` is also available as an alias for the same command – both spellings do the same thing.

The command requires you to be in a Git repository, because it orients itself by the Git root, and that Cursor is installed locally as an editor, so there's actually something to open. Typically you use `/open` when you're running a CLI session in the terminal but want to continue visually after finishing the work – for example to check changes in the diff view or edit files directly instead of tracing every change individually in the terminal.

whenGood.title: Continue visually after CLI work
whenGood.example: /open — after the agent has proposed the changes

whenGood.title: Continue editing a specific file in the editor
whenGood.example: /open, to manually refine a file changed by the agent directly in the Cursor editor

whenBad.title: Cursor (the editor) isn't installed or wanted at all
whenBad.why: /open requires a local Cursor installation.
whenBad.alternative: check changes directly in the terminal instead, e.g. with git diff

whenBad.title: No Git repository present
whenBad.why: According to the docs, /open opens the repository's Git root directory — without a Git repo there's no Git root to open.
whenBad.alternative: open the folder manually in the editor or stay in the normal terminal workflow

commands.name: /copy-request-id
commands.summary: Copies the last request's ID to the clipboard.
commands.what:
`/copy-request-id` copies the ID of the last request sent to the model to the clipboard. Unlike the conversation ID, which identifies the entire session, this request ID always refers only to the last single request within the session.

The command is mainly intended for support and debugging cases: when a specific problem occurs with exactly one response — an error, an unusually long response time, or an unexpected result — it can be reported precisely to the Cursor team via the request ID, without having to search through the entire session.

As with the other copy commands, there's no visible terminal output; the ID goes straight to the system clipboard. If the problem instead spans multiple messages or affects the whole session, `/copy-conversation-id` is the better choice.

whenGood.title: Report a specific problem to support
whenGood.example: /copy-request-id — paste the ID directly into the support ticket

whenGood.title: Make an unusual single response instantly traceable
whenGood.example: Run /copy-request-id right after a faulty response to capture the ID immediately

whenBad.title: It's about the whole conversation, not a single request
whenBad.why: The request ID refers only to the last single request.
whenBad.alternative: Use /copy-conversation-id instead

commands.name: /copy-conversation-id
commands.summary: Copies the current conversation's ID to the clipboard.
commands.what:
`/copy-conversation-id` copies the current chat session's unique ID to the clipboard. This ID identifies the entire conversation and differs from the request ID, which only identifies a single request within the session.

In practice, the command is mainly needed for support requests and debugging: if you report a problem that occurs across multiple messages or relates to the session as a whole, the conversation ID helps the Cursor team trace your session precisely. The ID is also useful for you personally, for example to find a session again later when you have several `cursor-agent` sessions open in parallel.

The command produces no visible terminal output; it places the ID directly on the system clipboard. You then need to paste it elsewhere, for example into a support ticket or a note.

whenGood.title: Find or reference a session later by its ID
whenGood.example: /copy-conversation-id — save the ID in a note before switching to another session

whenGood.title: Report a problem spanning multiple sessions to Cursor support
whenGood.example: Run /copy-conversation-id and paste the ID into the support ticket when the error spans multiple messages

commands.name: /logout
commands.summary: Signs out of the current Cursor account.
commands.what:
`/logout` signs you out of the currently logged-in account in the Cursor CLI. According to the reference table, the short description is "Sign out from Cursor"; the separate parameter documentation for the corresponding CLI subcommand (`agent logout`, callable outside the interactive session) specifies this as "Sign out and clear stored authentication" – the command thus also removes the locally stored credentials, not just the active session.

After `/logout` you're no longer signed in; the next time you use the CLI, you need to sign in again before you can make requests to models.

This makes `/logout` useful when you want to switch accounts or leave a shared computer clean – the stored authentication doesn't persist afterward.

whenGood.example: /logout — before switching to a different Cursor account, so no stored authentication remains

whenBad.title: You just want to end the session briefly, not sign out of the account
whenBad.why: /logout deletes the stored login; afterward a new login process is required.
whenBad.alternative: Use /quit or /exit to just end the session

commands.name: /quit
commands.summary: Exits the current CLI session.
commands.what:
`/quit` ends the current interactive session of the Cursor CLI. As with `/exit`, the description in the official slash command reference is simply "Exit" — according to the doc, the two commands are therefore interchangeable, neither has a documented additional benefit.

The reference doesn't mention arguments or options. After `/quit`, the chat process closes and you're back at the normal terminal.

If the session should be findable again later, `/rename` beforehand helps give it a recognizable name; it can then be reopened via `/resume` from the list of recent chats.

whenGood.title: The work is done
whenGood.example: After the last accepted change set, type `/quit` to close the chat.

whenGood.title: Use the more memorable command
whenGood.example: Those who find `/quit` easier to remember than `/exit` simply type `/quit` — according to the doc, identical behavior.

whenBad.title: Continuing work on exactly this session later
whenBad.why: After exiting, the session first has to be found again via `/resume` in the list of recent chats.
whenBad.alternative: Use `/rename` beforehand to make it easier to find later.

commands.name: /exit
commands.summary: Exits the current CLI session, identical to /quit.
commands.what:
`/exit` ends the current interactive session of the Cursor CLI (`cursor-agent`). You type the command into the prompt field without further arguments. In the official slash command reference, the description for `/exit` is identical to that for `/quit`: both are documented there simply as "Exit", so according to the doc there's no functional difference.

The reference doesn't mention options or arguments. After invoking it, the chat process ends and you land back at the normal terminal prompt.

If you want to continue working on the same session later, you can find it again via `/resume` — beforehand, a `/rename` is worthwhile so it stays recognizable in the list of recent chats.

whenGood.title: End the session after finishing
whenGood.example: After the last accepted commit, type `/exit` to leave the chat and return to the shell.

whenGood.title: Exit out of terminal habit
whenGood.example: Those used to `exit` from Unix terminals type `/exit` instead of `/quit` — according to the doc, identical behavior.

whenBad.title: Mixing both commands indiscriminately
whenBad.why: According to the reference, both `/exit` and `/quit` are described only as "Exit"; there's no documented difference.
whenBad.alternative: Use one of the two commands consistently.

`/copy` is a slash command within the running Cursor CLI session. According to the official reference table, it copies an earlier message of yours from the history to the clipboard; you select the desired message from a list.

The changelog from June 22, 2026 describes an extended version: via a picker, you can additionally select a single step from a multi-part agent response, so `/copy` can also copy the agent's responses in addition to your own messages; copying long responses also now works without the terminal hanging.

The short description in the slash commands reference is thus more limited than what the changelog describes in terms of functionality — so don't rely on `/copy` capturing only your own messages.

commands.name: /bedrock
commands.summary: Configures AWS Bedrock as the model backend, if the Bedrock feature is enabled.
commands.what:
`/bedrock [subcommand]` configures AWS Bedrock as the model backend for the Cursor CLI. According to the reference table, the command only works if the Bedrock feature is enabled for your account – if not, it has no effect.

According to Cursor's changelog, you use it to set up Bedrock "with your own credentials": either via classic AWS access keys or via a team IAM role. According to the changelog, the setup applies across the board – it works in interactive sessions as well as in headless mode and in editor integrations, so you don't have to configure Bedrock separately for each mode.

`/bedrock` is intended for setups where model requests should run over your own AWS infrastructure instead of Cursor's standard backend, for example for compliance or cost reasons in an enterprise environment.

commands.summary: Adds another directory to a multi-root session at runtime.
commands.what: /add-dir adds an extra directory to the running session to work across multiple repos at once. Slash skills and custom commands from the new directory refresh immediately; a restart is only needed for the agent to auto-discover new skills. commands.name: /save-workspace
commands.summary: Saves the currently active multi-root directories as a named workspace set.
commands.what:
`/save-workspace` saves the set of directories currently added via `/add-dir` as a named workspace set. According to Cursor's changelog, the command belongs to the "Named multi-directory workspaces" feature: it lets you have the agent work across multiple repositories at once, instead of only in the current directory.

You later reload the directory set saved this way via `/load-workspace` – according to the changelog, a global `--workspace` parameter is also available, to start a CLI session specifically targeted from the outset, instead of first assembling directories afterward via `/add-dir`.

`/save-workspace` is so far only documented in the June 22, 2026 changelog entry, not in the main reference table of slash commands – the same gap that, according to the task description, already existed for `/load-workspace`.

whenGood.title: Name a recurring repo combination
whenGood.example: /save-workspace backend-plus-shared-lib, after both directories were added via /add-dir

whenGood.title: Permanently bundle multiple repositories for a cross-repo task
whenGood.example: Collect directories with /add-dir and then save them with /save-workspace, to reload them later via /load-workspace

whenBad.title: The directory combination is only needed once
whenBad.why: For a one-off session, saving it as a named set isn't worth it.
whenBad.alternative: Simply use /add-dir without /save-workspace

whenBad.title: A session should start from the outset with a fixed directory selection
whenBad.why: /save-workspace only saves a directory set that has already been assembled in the chat, after the fact.
whenBad.alternative: Start the session directly with the --workspace parameter

commands.name: /load-workspace
commands.summary: Loads a multi-root workspace set previously saved with /save-workspace.
commands.what:
`/load-workspace` reloads a set of multiple directories previously saved with `/save-workspace` into the current session. According to the changelog entry from June 22, 2026 ("Named multi-directory workspaces"), this lets you use the agent across multiple repositories: you add directories at runtime with `/add-dir`, save the resulting set under a name with `/save-workspace`, and reopen it later with `/load-workspace`.

Alternatively, you start directly with a specific set via the `--workspace <path>` flag.

The command doesn't appear yet in the CLI doc's slash command reference table — it's only documented in the changelog. The entry doesn't specify finer syntax details, such as whether a name is required as an argument when loading.

whenGood.title: Return to the familiar multi-repo environment
whenGood.example: After restarting the CLI, call `/load-workspace` to reload the previously saved set of frontend and backend repos.

whenGood.title: Switch between cross-project setups
whenGood.example: Use `/load-workspace` for a context switch from one microservice set to another, instead of re-adding each directory with `/add-dir`.

whenBad.title: There's no saved set yet
whenBad.why: According to the changelog, the command requires a prior `/save-workspace` call.
whenBad.alternative: First add directories with `/add-dir` and save them with `/save-workspace`.

commands.name: agent logout
commands.summary: Signs the CLI out of your Cursor account and clears locally stored credentials.
commands.what:
agent logout is a top-level command from the CLI reference and signs the current CLI installation out of the Cursor account ("Sign out and clear stored authentication"). Afterward, the locally stored credentials are removed, and another agent login is required for the next use.

The official docs don't specify in detail how the credentials are technically stored — the authentication reference only states that credentials are "securely stored locally" after login, without naming a keychain or a specific storage variable. For scripts and CI environments, authentication can alternatively be provided entirely without an interactive login via the CURSOR_API_KEY environment variable or the --api-key <key> flag, which usually makes a logout unnecessary there.

agent status (alias: agent whoami) is a top-level command from the CLI reference and shows the current authentication status. According to the authentication reference, the output includes whether you're signed in, your account information, and the current endpoint configuration — relevant, for example, with differing or self-hosted API endpoints.

The --format <format> flag lets you choose between text (default) and json, which makes the output machine-readable and works well for scripts or CI checks. According to the docs, status and whoami are fully synonymous; both call the same function. The command doesn't change anything about the sign-in itself, it only reads out the current state.

commands.name: agent mcp
commands.summary: Parent command for managing configured MCP servers (login, list, tools, enable/disable).
commands.what: agent mcp groups all subcommands for managing Model Context Protocol servers: login, list, list-tools, enable, disable. The CLI uses the same mcp.json configuration as the Cursor editor (project and global level) and picks up servers from parent directories automatically. agent mcp list (or /mcp list in interactive mode) opens an interactive selection menu.

whenGood.title: Get an overview of which MCP servers are configured at all
whenGood.example: agent mcp list

whenGood.title: Skip all MCP approval prompts during a scripted run
whenGood.example: agent --approve-mcps -p "query my database for recent errors"

whenBad.title: An MCP tool should be used directly, not just managed
whenBad.why: agent mcp only manages server configuration, it doesn't call tools itself.
whenBad.alternative: Send a normal prompt to agent or agent -p — MCP tools are picked up automatically when relevant

whenBad.title: A new MCP server needs to be set up for the first time
whenBad.why: agent mcp only manages servers already entered in mcp.json.
whenBad.alternative: First add the server to .cursor/mcp.json or ~/.cursor/mcp.json, then approve it with agent mcp enable

commands.name: agent sandbox
commands.summary: Parent command, hidden from default help, for configuring sandbox mode or running one command in isolation.
commands.what: agent sandbox groups the enable, disable, reset, and run subcommands, which configure the CLI's sandbox mode or run a single command in isolation. Per the docs, agent sandbox is 'hidden' as a top-level command and therefore doesn't show up in default help (agent help). The same configuration can also be controlled interactively via /sandbox or the --sandbox <mode> flag.

whenGood.title: Turn on sandbox mode globally for all future sessions
whenGood.example: agent sandbox enable

whenGood.title: Test a single, potentially risky command in isolation
whenGood.example: agent sandbox run npm install

whenBad.title: Sandbox mode should only apply to a single session
whenBad.why: agent sandbox enable/disable changes a persistent setting that carries over across sessions.
whenBad.alternative: Set --sandbox enabled or --sandbox disabled only for that one agent call

whenBad.title: You just want to check which sandbox mode is currently active
whenBad.why: agent sandbox with no subcommand opens a configuration menu directly instead of just displaying status.
whenBad.alternative: Open /sandbox in interactive mode and view the current state there without changing anything

commands.name: agent worker
commands.summary: Parent command for starting a private cloud worker that runs agent tasks in your own environment.
commands.what: agent worker connects your own machine to Cursor and lets cloud-agent tasks run there instead of in Cursor's own cloud environment (self-hosted). Contains the start and debug subcommands. The worker is configured via flags like --worker-dir, --name, --label or --labels-file, --pool or --pool-name, and --idle-release-timeout.

whenGood.title: Provide your own hardware/environment for cloud-agent runs (privacy, special tooling)
whenGood.example: agent worker start --name build-worker-1 --worker-dir ~/repos/myapp

whenGood.title: Register several workers as a pool that cloud agents can draw from
whenGood.example: agent worker start --pool --pool-name ci-pool

whenBad.title: Only a single local agent run is needed
whenBad.why: agent worker starts a long-running process connected to Cursor for cloud-agent handoffs, not a one-off run.
whenBad.alternative: Use a normal interactive session with agent or agent -p

whenBad.title: Configuration/connectivity should be checked before actually starting
whenBad.why: agent worker start connects immediately; auth, privacy, or routing problems only surface afterwards.
whenBad.alternative: Run agent worker debug first to see preflight diagnostics

commands.name: agent acp
commands.summary: Starts the CLI in ACP server mode (Agent Client Protocol) for editor and client integrations.
commands.what: agent acp starts Cursor Agent as an ACP server over stdio, using newline-delimited JSON-RPC 2.0 messages, e.g. for editor integrations like Zed or JetBrains. Per the docs the command is 'hidden' and meant for building custom clients, not normal terminal use. Authentication happens beforehand via agent login, --api-key/CURSOR_API_KEY, or --auth-token/CURSOR_AUTH_TOKEN; endpoint and TLS options (-e, -k) are appended before acp, e.g. agent -e https://api2.cursor.sh acp.

whenGood.title: Build a custom client or editor integration against Cursor Agent
whenGood.example: agent acp — then send initialize/session/new/session/prompt via JSON-RPC over stdin/stdout

whenGood.title: Authenticate up front with an API key instead of logging in through the ACP flow
whenGood.example: agent --api-key "$CURSOR_API_KEY" acp

whenBad.title: Normal terminal use without building a client
whenBad.why: agent acp only outputs raw JSON-RPC messages on stdout, not a readable chat UI.
whenBad.alternative: Just use agent (interactive mode) or agent -p for scripts

whenBad.title: External tools/data need to be made available to the agent
whenBad.why: ACP is for client integrations, not for wiring tools into the agent.
whenBad.alternative: Use agent mcp to connect MCP servers for tool access

commands.name: agent update
commands.summary: Updates Cursor Agent to the latest version.
commands.what: agent update downloads and installs the latest CLI version. Background auto-updates are enabled by default; /update does the same thing directly from a running interactive session.

whenGood.title: Manually update to the latest version, e.g. to use a new feature flag
whenGood.example: agent update

whenBad.title: Automatic background updates are unwanted (e.g. a pinned version in CI)
whenBad.why: agent update is a manual one-off command and doesn't affect auto-update behavior.
whenBad.alternative: Set --disable-auto-update to turn off background updates entirely (see Global Options)

commands.name: agent ls
commands.summary: Opens a list of previous chats to pick one to resume.
commands.what: agent ls shows previous chat sessions to choose from, similar to /resume in interactive mode. The name is a bit misleading: despite 'ls' it doesn't list files, it lists sessions.

whenGood.title: You're unsure which of the recent sessions to resume
whenGood.example: agent ls

whenBad.title: You already know it should be the most recently used session
whenBad.why: agent ls shows a selection list first, adding an extra step.
whenBad.alternative: Use agent resume or agent --continue to resume the last session directly

commands.name: agent resume
commands.summary: Resumes the most recently used chat session directly, without showing a selection list.
commands.what: agent resume loads the most recently used session, including its prior context, and continues the conversation there. It's equivalent to --continue or the /resume slash command, both of which are shorthand for --resume=-1.

whenGood.title: Pick up the last conversation directly after an interruption
whenGood.example: agent resume

whenBad.title: An older session, not the most recent one, needs to be resumed
whenBad.why: agent resume always loads only the most recently used session.
whenBad.alternative: Use agent ls to pick a specific earlier session, or set --resume [chatId] with a concrete ID

commands.name: agent create-chat
commands.summary: Creates a new, empty chat and returns its ID, e.g. for use in scripts.
commands.what: agent create-chat creates an empty chat session and prints its ID to the console, without starting an interactive session directly. The ID can then be targeted again with --resume [chatId], for example from a script.

whenGood.title: Reserve a session ID up front to address it later from a script via --resume
whenGood.example: CHAT_ID=$(agent create-chat); agent --resume "$CHAT_ID" -p "start task"

whenBad.title: You just want to jump in and start chatting with the agent right away
whenBad.why: agent create-chat only creates an empty session, it doesn't start a conversation.
whenBad.alternative: Just use agent or agent "<prompt>"

commands.name: agent generate-rule | agent rule
commands.summary: Walks through interactive prompts to generate a new Cursor rule.
commands.what: agent generate-rule (alias: agent rule) walks you through creating a new rule interactively, which then lands in the CLI's rules system (.cursor/rules). The CLI automatically loads rules from .cursor/rules and applies them at startup; AGENTS.md and CLAUDE.md at the project root are also read as rules.

whenGood.title: Capture recurring project behavior as a persistent rule
whenGood.example: agent generate-rule — e.g. create a rule for the project's preferred test runner

whenGood.title: Make team-wide conventions available consistently across all sessions
whenGood.example: agent rule — generate a rule about commit message format or branch naming

whenBad.title: The instruction only applies to the current session, not permanently
whenBad.why: A generated rule lands in .cursor/rules and applies project-wide to future sessions.
whenBad.alternative: Just state the instruction directly in the prompt instead of creating a rule

whenBad.title: An existing rule needs editing, not a new one
whenBad.why: agent generate-rule always creates a new rule via the interactive flow.
whenBad.alternative: Edit the file in .cursor/rules directly, or use /rules in interactive mode to browse and edit

commands.name: agent install-shell-integration
commands.summary: Installs the CLI's shell integration into ~/.zshrc.
commands.what:
`agent install-shell-integration` is not a slash command inside a running chat session but a standalone terminal subcommand of the Cursor CLI. You run it directly in the shell, independent of a `cursor-agent` session, not as a `/` command in the chat.

The command sets up the shell integration by adding matching entries to `~/.zshrc`. According to the official docs, this explicitly refers to zsh; no separate integration routine is documented for other shells like bash, even though the regular installation of the CLI itself supports both bash and zsh according to the setup guide.

You typically run the command once after installing the CLI so Cursor Agent is cleanly wired into your shell environment, for example for autocomplete or context features. If you want to remove the integration again later, use its counterpart `agent uninstall-shell-integration`.

whenGood.title: Set up the shell integration once after installing the CLI
whenGood.example: agent install-shell-integration

whenGood.title: Check after a CLI update whether the integration is still wired up cleanly
whenGood.example: Run agent install-shell-integration again if shell features no longer work as expected.

whenBad.title: The shell integration should be removed again
whenBad.why: agent install-shell-integration only installs, it doesn't remove anything.
whenBad.alternative: Use agent uninstall-shell-integration

whenBad.title: You're not using a zsh shell
whenBad.why: According to the docs, the command explicitly targets ~/.zshrc; no integration routine is documented for other shells.
whenBad.alternative: Use Cursor CLI normally regardless — the shell integration is optional, not a requirement for it to work

commands.name: agent uninstall-shell-integration
commands.summary: Removes the CLI's shell integration from ~/.zshrc again.
commands.what:
`agent uninstall-shell-integration`, like its counterpart `agent install-shell-integration`, is not a slash command in the chat but a standalone terminal subcommand that you run directly in the shell, not inside a running `cursor-agent` session.

The command reverses the shell integration setup and removes the entries it added from `~/.zshrc`. According to the docs, only zsh is explicitly listed as a supported shell here as well.

The command is useful if the shell integration is causing problems, such as conflicts with other tools in your `.zshrc`, or if you want to remove Cursor CLI completely from your system and cleanly reset the shell configuration in the process. It removes the integration entirely rather than just disabling it — for a temporary pause, it's the wrong tool; manually commenting out the relevant block is better suited for that.

whenGood.title: Cleanly reset the shell integration when it's causing problems
whenGood.example: agent uninstall-shell-integration

whenGood.title: Fully uninstall Cursor CLI and clean up the shell configuration too
whenGood.example: Run agent uninstall-shell-integration before actually uninstalling the CLI

whenBad.title: The shell integration should only be paused briefly, not removed
whenBad.why: agent uninstall-shell-integration deletes the configuration completely instead of just disabling it.
whenBad.alternative: Manually comment out the relevant block in ~/.zshrc

commands.name: agent help [command]
commands.summary: Shows help for the CLI or for a specific command.
commands.what: agent help [command] shows general help, or, with a command name as argument, detailed help for exactly that command. It's functionally equivalent to the global -h/--help flag, which can be used on any individual command.

whenGood.title: Look up the available options of a subcommand
whenGood.example: agent help worker

whenBad.title: You just want to quickly see the options of the command you're already typing
whenBad.why: agent help command means a separate call instead of appending it right to the command.
whenBad.alternative: Append -h or --help directly to the command, e.g. agent worker --help

commands.name: agent mcp login <identifier>
commands.summary: Authenticates with an MCP server configured in mcp.json.
commands.what: agent mcp login <identifier> starts a login flow with automatic callback handling for an MCP server configured in .cursor/mcp.json or ~/.cursor/mcp.json. Once login succeeds, the agent immediately has access to the server's authenticated tools.

whenGood.title: Make an MCP server with its own authentication (e.g. OAuth) usable for the first time
whenGood.example: agent mcp login linear

whenBad.title: The server is already configured but just needs to be approved locally
whenBad.why: agent mcp login handles authentication, not approving the server.
whenBad.alternative: Use agent mcp enable <identifier>

commands.name: agent mcp list
commands.summary: Lists configured MCP servers and their status (connected/disconnected, source, transport).
commands.what: agent mcp list opens an interactive menu with all configured MCP servers: name, connection status, configuration source (project or global), and transport method (stdio, HTTP, SSE). In interactive mode /mcp list gives the same overview.

whenGood.title: Check which MCP servers are currently connected before a task
whenGood.example: agent mcp list

whenBad.title: You want to see the parameters of a specific tool, not just the server list
whenBad.why: agent mcp list only shows server status, no tool details.
whenBad.alternative: Use agent mcp list-tools <identifier> for a specific server

commands.name: agent mcp list-tools <identifier>
commands.summary: Lists the available tools and their parameters for a specific MCP server.
commands.what:
`agent mcp list-tools <identifier>` is a terminal subcommand of the Cursor CLI — you call it as `cursor-agent mcp list-tools <identifier>` directly in the shell, not as a slash command within a running session. Within a session, `/mcp list-tools` provides comparable functionality.

The command shows all tools provided by a single, already-configured MCP server: names, descriptions, and the associated parameters with required/optional status and type. The `<identifier>` corresponds to the server name from your `mcp.json`; names with spaces are also supported.

This distinguishes the command from `agent mcp list`, which only lists the configured servers along with connection status but doesn't provide tool details. The configuration follows the same precedence order as in the editor: project before global before nested.

whenGood.title: Check parameters before using an MCP tool for the first time
whenGood.example: cursor-agent mcp list-tools playwright

whenGood.title: Check which tools a server offers now after changes to mcp.json
whenGood.example: cursor-agent mcp list-tools github

whenBad.title: You don't know the server identifier yet
whenBad.why: agent mcp list-tools requires a specific identifier as an argument.
whenBad.alternative: use cursor-agent mcp list first to see the configured identifiers

whenBad.title: You just want to quickly know whether a server is connected at all
whenBad.why: list-tools shows tool details, not a server's connection status.
whenBad.alternative: use cursor-agent mcp list

commands.name: agent mcp enable <identifier>
commands.summary: Adds an MCP server to the locally approved list.
commands.what:
agent mcp enable <identifier> is a subcommand from the "agent mcp" category (MCP server management) and, according to the Cursor docs, permanently adds an already configured MCP server to the locally approved list, so it loads in future without another approval prompt. <identifier> refers to a server that was previously entered in a .cursor/mcp.json (project) or ~/.cursor/mcp.json (global).

Sibling subcommands are agent mcp list (shows configured servers and their status), agent mcp list-tools <identifier> (shows a server's available tools), agent mcp login <identifier> (authenticates against a server), and agent mcp disable <identifier> as the counterpart to enable. According to the changelog, an enable/disable also takes immediate effect on the available tools from within a running session (via /mcp), with no restart needed.

whenGood.title: Permanently approve an already trusted server
whenGood.example: agent mcp enable github

whenGood.title: Check which servers are even configured before approving
whenGood.example: Run agent mcp list, note the relevant identifier, then call agent mcp enable <identifier>

whenBad.title: Approve all configured servers at once for a single script run
whenBad.why: agent mcp enable only takes effect per server and permanently, not for a single run.
whenBad.alternative: Set --approve-mcps as a global flag on the respective agent call, e.g. agent --approve-mcps "..."

whenBad.title: The server isn't entered in an mcp.json yet
whenBad.why: enable only unlocks already configured servers, it doesn't create a new server.
whenBad.alternative: First enter the server in .cursor/mcp.json or ~/.cursor/mcp.json, then use agent mcp enable

commands.name: agent mcp disable <identifier>
commands.summary: Disables an MCP server so it stops loading or prompting for approval.
commands.what:
`agent mcp disable <identifier>` is a terminal subcommand — called as `cursor-agent mcp disable <identifier>` directly in the shell, not a slash command. It fully disables an already-configured MCP server: afterward, the server is neither loaded at startup nor does the CLI ask for approval for it in the future.

The counterpart is `agent mcp enable <identifier>`, which puts a server back on the locally approved list. The same action can alternatively be performed within a running session via the interactive detail view of `/mcp` — that view also offers login, logout with deletion of stored OAuth credentials, enable, and disable per server.

The setting applies server-wide and persistently, not just for the current request or session — it stays in effect until you re-enable the server.

whenGood.title: Turn off a faulty or unneeded MCP server
whenGood.example: cursor-agent mcp disable old-server

whenGood.title: Hide an internal/experimental server before a demo so it doesn't keep asking for approval
whenGood.example: cursor-agent mcp disable playwright-experimental

whenBad.title: The server should only be ignored briefly for one run
whenBad.why: agent mcp disable is a persistent, server-bound setting.
whenBad.alternative: simply don't include the server in the relevant prompt, or adjust the project-specific mcp.json

whenBad.title: You only want to log the server out temporarily for testing but keep stored OAuth credentials
whenBad.why: disable only changes the load/approval status, not the credentials.
whenBad.alternative: Open the detail view via /mcp and choose Logout specifically instead of Disable there, if credentials should be removed

commands.name: agent sandbox enable
commands.summary: Enables sandbox mode for command execution.
commands.what: agent sandbox enable turns sandbox mode on: commands then run with read/write access to the workspace but isolated from the rest of the system (network disabled by default). The setting persists across sessions.

whenGood.title: Turn on persistently isolated command execution for all future sessions
whenGood.example: agent sandbox enable

whenBad.title: The sandbox should only apply to a single command, not permanently
whenBad.why: agent sandbox enable changes the persistent configuration for all future runs.
whenBad.alternative: Use agent sandbox run <cmd> to run just one command in isolation

commands.name: agent sandbox disable
commands.summary: Disables sandbox mode and falls back to allowlist mode instead.
commands.what: agent sandbox disable turns sandbox mode off. The CLI then falls back to allowlist mode, where individual commands must be approved manually instead of running isolated automatically.

whenGood.title: Sandbox restrictions (e.g. no network) permanently get in the way of a particular workflow
whenGood.example: agent sandbox disable

whenBad.title: Network access is only needed for a single sandboxed run
whenBad.why: agent sandbox disable turns off the sandbox entirely instead of just allowing network.
whenBad.alternative: Use agent sandbox run <cmd> --network to allow network access just for that run

commands.name: agent sandbox reset
commands.summary: Resets the sandbox configuration to its default values.
commands.what:
agent sandbox reset is a subcommand from the "agent sandbox" category and resets individual changes to the sandbox configuration back to the default values ("Reset sandbox configuration to defaults").

Sibling subcommands are agent sandbox enable (enable sandbox mode for command execution), agent sandbox disable (disable the sandbox and use allowlist mode instead), and agent sandbox run <cmd> [args...], which lets you run a single command with workspace read/write access inside a sandbox; run additionally comes with a --network flag that defaults to false. According to Cursor's general sandbox configuration reference, the default filesystem access is "workspace_readwrite" and the default network rule is "deny", meaning network access is blocked by default unless explicitly allowed.

whenGood.title: Restore a clean starting state after several experiments with paths or network rules
whenGood.example: Run agent sandbox reset after repeatedly experimenting with sandbox enable/disable and network settings

whenGood.title: Make sure no old sandbox customizations remain active before a new project
whenGood.example: agent sandbox reset, followed by agent sandbox enable, to start with a guaranteed clean configuration

whenBad.title: Only a single setting should be changed, not all of them
whenBad.why: agent sandbox reset resets the entire configuration, not just a single value.
whenBad.alternative: Use agent sandbox enable/disable or the --network flag on agent sandbox run in a targeted way

commands.name: agent sandbox run <cmd> [args...]
commands.summary: Runs a single command in a sandbox with read/write access to the workspace.
commands.what: agent sandbox run <cmd> [args...] runs exactly one command in isolation, by default with read/write access to the workspace (--sandbox, default true) and no network access (--network, default false). Extra paths can be exposed via --allow-paths or --readonly-paths, and unwanted files blocked via --blocked-patterns (gitignore syntax); --sb-debug writes debug logs to a temp folder.

whenGood.title: Test an unfamiliar install/build script in isolation before it touches the real workspace
whenGood.example: agent sandbox run npm install

whenGood.title: Run a command with network access even though the sandbox otherwise blocks it
whenGood.example: agent sandbox run --network curl https://example.com/healthz

whenBad.title: Several commands need to run isolated persistently, not just one
whenBad.why: agent sandbox run is meant for exactly one single command.
whenBad.alternative: Use agent sandbox enable so the sandbox policy applies to all future commands the CLI runs

whenBad.title: The command needs access outside the workspace directory
whenBad.why: Without extra flags, access is limited to the workspace.
whenBad.alternative: Specify --allow-paths or --readonly-paths with the additionally needed paths

commands.name: agent sandbox help [command]
commands.summary: Shows help for the sandbox subcommands.
commands.what:
`agent sandbox help [command]` is a terminal subcommand — called as `cursor-agent sandbox help [command]`, not as a slash command. It shows help text for the `agent sandbox` subcommands: `enable`, `disable`, `reset`, and `run <cmd> [args...]`. Without an argument, it lists all four; with a subcommand as an argument, it shows that subcommand's details, such as the options for `run`.

Sandbox mode itself runs commands in a restricted environment that blocks file access and network activity by default (`--network` defaults to `false`, `--sandbox` defaults to `true`). Via `run`, you can specify additional read/write paths (`--allow-paths`), read-only paths (`--readonly-paths`), and gitignore-style blocking patterns (`--blocked-patterns`); `--sb-debug` writes sandbox debug logs to a temp folder.

Distinct from this is the interactive slash command `/sandbox`, which opens a menu for configuring sandbox mode within the session.

whenGood.title: Look up the available options for sandbox run
whenGood.example: cursor-agent sandbox help run

whenGood.title: Get an overview of all sandbox subcommands
whenGood.example: cursor-agent sandbox help

whenBad.title: Quickly see only the options of the sandbox command you're currently typing
whenBad.why: agent sandbox help command is a separate call.
whenBad.alternative: append -h or --help directly, e.g. cursor-agent sandbox run --help

whenBad.title: Interactively toggling sandbox mode for the current session
whenBad.why: agent sandbox help only shows help text and doesn't change any setting.
whenBad.alternative: use /sandbox within the running session

commands.name: agent worker start
commands.summary: Starts the private worker and connects it to Cursor.
commands.what: agent worker start starts the private worker process and connects it to Cursor, so cloud-agent tasks run in your own environment instead of Cursor's cloud. It's configured via flags like --worker-dir (workspace root, repeatable, the first value sets the assignment identity), --name, --label/--labels-file, --pool/--pool-name, --idle-release-timeout, and --management-addr for /healthz, /readyz, /metrics. --verbose enables verbose startup logs.

whenGood.title: Expose several repos at once as worker workspaces
whenGood.example: agent worker start --worker-dir ~/repos/app-a --worker-dir ~/repos/app-b

whenGood.title: Expose health/metrics endpoints for monitoring the worker
whenGood.example: agent worker start --management-addr 0.0.0.0:9100

whenBad.title: You want to check up front whether auth and network would even work
whenBad.why: agent worker start connects live immediately, without a dry-run check first.
whenBad.alternative: Run agent worker debug first, then agent worker start

whenBad.title: Only a single, short agent run is needed
whenBad.why: agent worker start starts a long-running process connected to Cursor.
whenBad.alternative: Use a normal session with agent or agent -p instead of running a worker

commands.name: agent worker debug
commands.summary: Runs preflight diagnostics for the private worker (auth, privacy, routing).
commands.what: agent worker debug checks the private worker's authentication, privacy settings, and routing before actually starting it, and prints a diagnostic report. --json outputs the report as machine-readable JSON.

whenGood.title: Catch configuration mistakes before the first production start of a new worker
whenGood.example: agent worker debug --json

whenBad.title: The worker should just run in production directly, without a prior check
whenBad.why: agent worker debug doesn't start the worker, it only checks the prerequisites.
whenBad.alternative: Use agent worker start directly once the configuration is already known to work

commands.name: agent worker help [command]
commands.summary: Shows help for the worker subcommands.
commands.what:
`agent worker help [command]` is a terminal subcommand — called as `cursor-agent worker help [command]` in the shell, not a slash command. It shows help text for the `agent worker` subcommands `start` and `debug`; without an argument, it lists both, and with either of the two as an argument, it shows that subcommand's details along with its flags.

A worker is a self-hosted instance that establishes a persistent outgoing HTTPS connection to Cursor's cloud and executes terminal commands, file changes, and other tool calls there on your own infrastructure — for example, for cloud agents or as a personal 'My Machines' machine. `agent worker start` registers and starts this connection, among other things with flags like `--pool`, `--worker-dir`, `--label`, or `--idle-release-timeout`. `agent worker debug` checks authentication, privacy routing, repo labels, and whether Cursor sees matching workers at all, ahead of time.

whenGood.title: Look up the available flags for worker start, e.g. for pool configuration
whenGood.example: cursor-agent worker help start

whenGood.title: Check what worker debug actually controls before using it in production
whenGood.example: cursor-agent worker help debug

whenBad.title: Quickly see only the options of the worker command you're currently typing
whenBad.why: agent worker help command is a separate call.
whenBad.alternative: append -h or --help directly, e.g. cursor-agent worker start --help

whenBad.title: You want to directly start or test a worker
whenBad.why: agent worker help only shows help text but doesn't connect a worker to Cursor.
whenBad.alternative: run cursor-agent worker start or cursor-agent worker debug directly

commands.name: agent bedrock
commands.summary: Configures AWS Bedrock as a model backend with your own credentials or a team IAM role.
commands.what: Documented in the official changelog, not (yet) in the command reference table. Per the changelog entry (February 2026), agent bedrock configures access to AWS Bedrock either via your own access keys or a team IAM role, and works across interactive, headless, and editor sessions. As the slash command /bedrock it is additionally listed in the slash command reference doc; as a top-level CLI subcommand it's missing from reference/parameters.

whenGood.title: Set up Bedrock as a bring-your-own-key model backend instead of Cursor's default models
whenGood.example: agent bedrock

whenBad.title: You just want to switch the model for one run, not the backend
whenBad.why: agent bedrock configures the backend itself, not just a single model for one session.
whenBad.alternative: Use --model <model> or /model if you only need to pick a different already-available model

commands.name: Global Options (Flags)
commands.summary: Collects the most important global flags of the Cursor CLI that can be combined with any command.
commands.what:
Global options can be combined with any command (agent, agent mcp list, agent sandbox run, ...). The most important ones:
-p, --print: non-interactive mode, prints the response to the console (for scripts/CI); has full access to write and shell
--output-format <format>: text (default), json, or stream-json — only works together with --print
--model <model>: sets the model to use
--mode <mode>: plan or ask (default is full agent mode when this flag is omitted); --plan is shorthand for --mode=plan
-f, --force (alias --yolo): auto-allows commands unless explicitly denied — skips approval prompts
--sandbox <mode>: enabled or disabled
--approve-mcps: automatically approves all configured MCP servers
--trust: trusts the workspace without prompting (headless/print mode only)
--add-dir <path>: adds an extra directory for a multi-root session at startup (changelog-only)
--auto-review: enables auto-review execution mode, a classifier decides approvals instead of a fixed allowlist (changelog-only)
--image: attaches an image to the session (changelog-only)
-w, --worktree [name]: runs the agent in a new Git worktree instead of editing the current checkout directly
--resume [chatId] / --continue: resumes an existing or the most recently used chat session
--workspace <path>: sets the project directory to use
-h, --help: shows help for the given command

whenGood.title: Use -p in scripts and CI pipelines
whenGood.example: agent -p "find and fix performance issues" --model "gpt-5" --output-format json

whenGood.title: Combine flags deliberately instead of picking an unnecessarily broad mode
whenGood.example: agent -p --mode ask "summarize the auth module" — read-only, structured output for a script

whenBad.title: Set --force/--yolo by default on every run without reviewing the changes
whenBad.why: This also auto-approves risky commands without anyone seeing them beforehand.
whenBad.alternative: Review changes deliberately after the run (Ctrl+R or /changes), or additionally set --sandbox enabled to at least isolate execution

whenBad.title: Set --mode ask but then expect file changes afterwards
whenBad.why: In ask mode the agent makes no file changes; a script expecting write access afterwards will find nothing happened.
whenBad.alternative: Use default agent mode (no --mode flag) for runs that need file changes, or --plan to plan ahead first

commands.name: /add
commands.summary: Adds one or more files to the chat so Aider can edit them or use them as detailed context.
commands.what: /add adds files to the current chat session. Aider can only edit files that are in the chat. If a new file that doesn't exist yet is given to /add, Aider remembers the filename and writes to it later instead of accidentally changing an existing file. Besides the added files, Aider also uses a map of the whole git repo, so it's aware of code outside the chat too.

whenGood.title: Make a file editable
whenGood.example: /add payment.py — add the file to the chat before asking Aider to change it

whenGood.title: Safely create a new file
whenGood.example: /add utils/newfile.py before asking Aider to write a new helper function there — this way the change lands in the new file instead of an existing one

whenBad.title: Adding many files just in case
whenBad.why: Too much irrelevant code in the chat distracts the LLM; the docs recommend adding only the files actually needed.
whenBad.alternative: Add only the 1-2 truly relevant files and let the automatic repo map cover the rest

whenBad.title: Only wanting to show a file as reference, not edit it
whenBad.why: /add makes files directly editable — unnecessary if the file should only serve as context.
whenBad.alternative: Use /read-only to add the file for reference only

commands.name: /architect
