commands.summary: Shows installed plugins and their loaded components.
commands.what: agy plugin list shows active plugin packages and the components they've loaded (e.g. skills, agents, MCP servers). Plugins follow the plugin.json schema with a required name field (alphanumeric, hyphens, underscores only) and an optional description field.

whenGood.title: Get an overview of currently installed plugins
whenGood.example: Run agy plugin list before a planned uninstall or update

whenBad.title: You want to enable/disable or remove a plugin
whenBad.why: list only shows the current state, it doesn't change anything.
whenBad.alternative: agy plugin enable/disable <name> or agy plugin uninstall <name>

commands.name: agy plugin install <path>
commands.summary: Installs a local or downloaded plugin directory.
commands.what: agy plugin install /path/to/local/plugin stages a plugin directory into your local profile. External plugin installs automatically resolve and initialize git submodules; installing directly from GitHub subpaths (with branch resolution) is also supported. The import copies the entire plugin directory, including non-skill subfolders like shared/.

whenGood.title: Wire in a locally developed plugin directory
whenGood.example: agy plugin install ./my-plugin

whenGood.title: Install a plugin straight from a GitHub repo or subpath
whenGood.example: agy plugin install github.com/org/repo/path/to/plugin

whenBad.title: You only want to bring over legacy Gemini CLI extensions
whenBad.why: plugin install expects a plugin in the native plugin.json format, not a Gemini CLI extension directly.
whenBad.alternative: Use agy plugin import gemini to convert extensions first

commands.name: agy plugin enable <name>
commands.summary: Reactivates a previously disabled plugin without reinstalling it.
commands.what:
`agy plugin enable <name>` is a terminal subcommand of the `agy` binary, not a slash command: you type it in your normal shell, not in the prompt box of the interactive session. It belongs to the Antigravity CLI's plugin management pipeline, which also includes `agy plugin list`, `agy plugin install`, `agy plugin disable`, `agy plugin uninstall`, and `agy plugin validate`.

The command reactivates a plugin that was previously paused with `agy plugin disable <name>`. According to the docs, the disable/enable pair serves to suspend a plugin's tools without deleting its files – enable reverses this suspension. The plugin must therefore already be installed: enable doesn't install anything new or reload any files, it just re-enables already existing tools and capabilities for the agent, without a renewed installation step.

whenGood.title: Make a paused plugin usable again
whenGood.example: agy plugin enable my-plugin — after you had previously paused it for testing with agy plugin disable

whenGood.title: Reactivate a specific plugin after taking stock
whenGood.example: Check agy plugin list to see which plugins are disabled, then run agy plugin enable <name> for one of them

whenBad.title: The plugin isn't installed yet
whenBad.why: enable only re-enables an already installed but disabled plugin — it has no effect for a new plugin.
whenBad.alternative: First use agy plugin install <path>, after that the plugin is active

commands.name: agy plugin disable <name>
commands.summary: Suspends a plugin without uninstalling it.
commands.what: agy plugin disable <plugin_name> suspends a plugin's tools without removing the plugin directory or its configuration. It can be reactivated at any time with agy plugin enable <name>.

whenGood.title: Switch a plugin off for testing without losing it
whenGood.example: agy plugin disable my-plugin to narrow down a conflict with another plugin

whenBad.title: The plugin should be removed permanently and completely
whenBad.why: disable leaves the directory and registry entries untouched.
whenBad.alternative: Use agy plugin uninstall <name>

commands.name: agy plugin uninstall <name>
commands.summary: Fully removes a plugin directory including its registry entries.
commands.what:
Strictly speaking, `agy plugin uninstall <name>` is not a slash command of the interactive TUI, but a CLI subcommand that you call directly in the terminal — that is, `agy plugin uninstall <plugin_name>`, not `/plugin uninstall` in the prompt window.

According to the official Antigravity CLI docs, the command removes a plugin completely: it "purges" the package directory and cleans up the associated registry entries. This clearly distinguishes it from `agy plugin disable`, which only temporarily suspends a plugin without deleting its files. The rest of plugin management also includes `agy plugin list` (shows active packages along with loaded components) and `agy plugin install` (moves a package directory into the local profile).

Use `uninstall` when a plugin should disappear for good. If you only want to temporarily deactivate it, `disable` is the gentler choice, because reactivating it later remains possible without reinstalling.

whenGood.title: Permanently remove a plugin that's no longer needed
whenGood.example: agy plugin uninstall my-plugin

whenGood.title: Clean up before a plugin gets replaced by a new version
whenGood.example: agy plugin uninstall old-plugin, followed by agy plugin install ./new-plugin

whenBad.title: The plugin should only be suspended temporarily
whenBad.why: uninstall completely removes the directory and registry entries; turning it back on later requires reinstalling.
whenBad.alternative: Use agy plugin disable <name>, which only suspends the tools without deleting the plugin files

commands.name: agy plugin import gemini
commands.summary: Automatically converts legacy Gemini CLI extensions into native Antigravity CLI plugins.
commands.what: agy plugin import gemini scans local Gemini CLI directories, reads the extension manifests, and converts them into the native plugin layout. Legacy commands get converted to skills, existing skills are carried over, and mcpServers entries migrate into a dedicated mcp_config.json; for remote servers you then need to rename the url/httpUrl schema key to serverUrl manually. The output lists per extension exactly what was converted, e.g. 'commands: 4 legacy commands converted to skills'.

whenGood.title: Automatically bring over existing extensions when switching from Gemini CLI
whenGood.example: Run agy plugin import gemini right after installing Antigravity CLI

whenBad.title: You want to install a single, brand-new plugin from scratch
whenBad.why: import gemini only converts existing legacy Gemini CLI extensions, not new plugins.
whenBad.alternative: Use agy plugin install <path>

sources.title: Antigravity CLI docs: Gemini CLI Migration

commands.name: install.sh --skip-aliases
commands.summary: Skips cleaning up old agy/antigravity shell aliases during install.
commands.what: The --skip-aliases flag is passed when running the install script (install.sh/install.ps1/install.cmd) and stops the script from cleaning up or updating existing legacy agy or antigravity shell aliases in your shell profile.

whenGood.title: Keep your own, manually maintained agy/antigravity shell aliases
whenGood.example: curl -fsSL https://antigravity.google/cli/install.sh | bash -s -- --skip-aliases

whenBad.title: Old, broken, or wrongly-pointed aliases are still in your shell profile
whenBad.why: With --skip-aliases, the installer specifically won't clean up those old aliases automatically.
whenBad.alternative: Run the installer without --skip-aliases so old aliases get cleaned up automatically

commands.name: install.sh --skip-path
commands.summary: Skips automatically appending PATH in your shell profile during install.
commands.what: The --skip-path flag is passed when running the install script and stops it from automatically appending the binary directory (~/.local/bin or %LOCALAPPDATA%\agy\bin) to PATH in your shell profile.

whenGood.title: Manage the PATH entry yourself, e.g. in an existing dotfiles setup
whenGood.example: curl -fsSL https://antigravity.google/cli/install.sh | bash -s -- --skip-path

whenBad.title: agy should be callable from any terminal right after installing, with no extra manual step
whenBad.why: Without the automatic PATH entry, the shell won't find the agy binary without a manual PATH change.
whenBad.alternative: Run the installer without --skip-path

commands.name: @<path>
commands.summary: Opens an interactive overlay for picking a file path right in the prompt box.
commands.what: Typing @ in the prompt box opens the Interactive Path Suggestion overlay: it lets you browse workspace file paths and insert one directly into your prompt as an absolute path, helping the agent search the code more precisely. Since 1.0.6, @ triggers suggestions unconditionally, including right after an opening parenthesis.

whenGood.title: Reference a specific file precisely without typing the path by hand
whenGood.example: Type @src/auth/ to browse to the right file in the overlay

whenBad.title: You want to run a terminal command directly
whenBad.why: @ only inserts a file path into the prompt, it doesn't execute anything.
whenBad.alternative: Use ! at the start of a line for direct terminal commands

sources.title: Antigravity CLI docs: Using the CLI

commands.name: !<shell-command>
commands.summary: Runs a terminal command directly from the prompt box.
commands.what:
A `!` at the start of the input in the prompt box is not a slash command, but a prefix. According to the official docs, you use `!` at the start of your prompt to execute terminal commands directly. The text that follows is executed one-to-one as a shell command instead of going to the agent as an instruction – the agent doesn't interpret or plan anything here, the command is passed straight through.

This makes the prefix comparable to other shortcuts in the prompt box, such as `@` for file path completion. Separately, there's a keyboard shortcut (`e`) that lets you edit terminal commands suggested by the agent itself before execution – but that applies to commands the agent proposes for approval, not to the manually typed !-prefix, which executes immediately without confirmation.

whenGood.title: Quickly run a known terminal command without leaving the TUI
whenGood.example: !git status or !ls, to take a quick look without involving the agent

whenGood.title: Test a command whose raw output you want to read yourself directly
whenGood.example: !npm run build, to see the unfiltered terminal result

whenBad.title: The agent should choose the right command itself or interpret the result
whenBad.why: ! executes the command directly and unchanged, without the agent selecting it, adapting it, or evaluating the result.
whenBad.alternative: Phrase the request as a normal prompt, so the agent suggests the appropriate command itself and interprets the result

sources.title: Antigravity CLI docs: Using the CLI

commands.summary: Shows help and a list of all slash commands.
commands.what:
According to the official Antigravity CLI docs, a `?` in the prompt box is not its own slash command with a `/` prefix, but a special-character shortcut: if you type just `?`, help opens with a list of all available slash commands.

This distinguishes `?` from real commands like `/config` or `/permissions`, which appear in the typeahead menu as soon as you type `/`. `?` serves purely as an overview — it doesn't perform any action itself, but shows you which `/` commands exist in your current version.

The official CLI reference also lists a separate `/help` command (category "Utilities"), which according to the docs opens a help panel with commands and shortcuts. `?` and `/help` overlap heavily in function; `?` is the faster reflex directly from the input line, without first typing out `/help`.

whenGood.title: Quickly check which slash commands are available in the current version
whenGood.example: Type ? in the prompt box before venturing into an unfamiliar workflow

whenGood.title: Quickly check the overview before typing `/`
whenGood.example: Type ? to see whether there's already a matching command for a specific task

whenBad.title: You already know the command and want to run it directly
whenBad.why: According to the docs, ? only opens the help overview, but doesn't perform any action itself.
whenBad.alternative: Type the known slash command directly, e.g. /tasks

whenBad.title: Expecting a standalone, named slash command
whenBad.why: According to the docs, ? is not a `/` command with its own name, but a separate help special character in the prompt box.
whenBad.alternative: Use /help if you'd rather reference a documented, named slash command

sources.title: Antigravity CLI docs: Using the CLI

commands.name: esc esc
commands.summary: Clears the prompt box, as long as no response is currently streaming.
commands.what:
`esc esc` refers to pressing the Escape key twice in the Antigravity CLI TUI — so it's a keyboard shortcut, not a slash command. According to the official "Using AGY CLI" page, this key combination clears the current input in the prompt box, but only when no response stream is currently active.

In the standard keybindings table, the Escape key is additionally mapped more generally to "stop stream, close menus, or clear prompt", while `esc esc` specifically covers quickly clearing a faulty or no-longer-needed input.

To cancel a running agent response stream, according to the changelog (version 1.0.11), `ctrl+c` is the documented means instead: the first press cancels the active action, a second press triggers the CLI's exit flow. Key combinations can be customized via `keybindings.json`, but `cli.exit` and `cli.enter` are excluded from this according to the docs.

whenGood.title: Quickly discard a faulty input
whenGood.example: Press esc esc to clear the currently typed but not yet submitted input

whenGood.title: Start over without a mouse
whenGood.example: After a botched copy-paste into the prompt box, press esc twice to type everything from scratch

whenBad.title: Wanting to cancel a running response stream
whenBad.why: According to the docs, esc esc only clears the prompt box and explicitly only works when no stream is active; ctrl+c is documented for canceling.
whenBad.alternative: Use ctrl+c to interrupt an active agent run

sources.title: Antigravity CLI docs: Using the CLI

commands.name: .agents/skills/*.md → /<skill-name>
commands.summary: Local or global markdown skills automatically become their own /<skill-name> slash commands.
commands.what: A markdown file with frontmatter (name, description) plus agent instructions in .agents/skills/ at the workspace root gets compiled the next time agy starts and is then available as /<skill-name> in the prompt box. The same applies globally to markdown files in ~/.gemini/antigravity-cli/skills/ — these are automatically imported as a global slash command across all workspaces. Migrating from Gemini CLI changes the paths: workspace-local moves from .gemini/skills/ to .agents/skills/, global moves from ~/.gemini/skills/ to ~/.gemini/antigravity-cli/skills/.

whenGood.title: Turn a recurring workflow into its own command for the project
whenGood.example: Add format-tests.md with frontmatter to .agents/skills/ so /format-tests shows up in the prompt box

whenGood.title: Use a skill across every project
whenGood.example: Put the skill file in ~/.gemini/antigravity-cli/skills/ instead

whenBad.title: Skills migrated from Gemini CLI still sit at the old path (.gemini/skills/ or ~/.gemini/skills/)
whenBad.why: Antigravity CLI only recognizes skills at the new paths (.agents/skills/ or ~/.gemini/antigravity-cli/skills/) — the old paths are no longer picked up.
whenBad.alternative: Move the skill files to the new path manually (agy plugin import gemini only converts extensions, not loose skill files)

sources.title: Antigravity CLI docs: Gemini CLI Migration

commands.name: /add-dir
commands.summary: Adds an extra directory to the active workspace.
commands.what: /add-dir belongs to the Utilities category of the central Antigravity CLI slash command reference. It extends the active workspace with another directory so the agent can access files outside the starting directory. It takes a path as an argument.

whenGood.title: Bring in code from a second repo or folder
whenGood.example: /add-dir ../shared-lib

whenGood.title: Add a monorepo sub-project to the session
whenGood.example: /add-dir packages/api

whenBad.title: You only need to reference a file once
whenBad.why: /add-dir permanently attaches an entire directory to the workspace; for a one-off reference, a file path in the prompt is enough.
whenBad.alternative: Use @<path> directly in the prompt

commands.name: /agents
commands.summary: Opens the agent manager panel to pick custom agents and monitor running subagents.
commands.what: /agents belongs to the Tools & Tasks category. In the panel, ↑/↓ navigate the list, Enter selects a custom agent or opens a subagent's detail view, k kills an active subagent, a approves and d denies inline tool requests right from the list, and Esc goes back. Complements the --agent startup flag and the agy agents subcommand.

whenGood.title: Switch between multiple custom agents
whenGood.example: Open /agents and use ↑/↓ + Enter to pick a different agent for the session

whenGood.title: Check on or cancel a running subagent task
whenGood.example: Open /agents, select a subagent, and kill it with k

whenBad.title: You just want a quick list of available custom agents
whenBad.why: /agents opens an interactive panel; for a plain list without panel interaction, the subcommand is enough.
whenBad.alternative: Run agy agents at startup

commands.name: /artifact
commands.summary: Opens the artifact review panel.
commands.what:
/artifact belongs to the Tools & Tasks category and opens the Artifact Review Panel — the central place where the Antigravity CLI presents the agent's deliverables to you for review. According to the docs, an artifact is a structured result the agent produces to accomplish its task and to communicate progress and reasoning to you: implementation plans as Markdown, code diffs, architecture diagrams, and media files.

As soon as the agent creates or modifies files, the status line shows "/artifact to review". The panel separates code files that require approval from a collapsible media drawer for images and videos. Use `↑`/`↓` to navigate between entries, `y` to approve a file, `n` to reject it, `Shift+A` approves all at once. In the detail view, use `c` to attach line-by-line comments before the change is written.

Alternatively, you can open the panel at any time via the `ctrl+r` shortcut, even while an agent question is still pending.

whenGood.title: Review agent-generated files before they're written
whenGood.example: Open /artifact (or `ctrl+r`) and use `y`/`n` to approve or reject individual agent-generated files before they get written to disk.

whenGood.title: Review an implementation plan or diagram
whenGood.example: After a larger task, call /artifact to read the agent-generated Markdown plan or an architecture diagram in detail and comment on it with `c`.

whenBad.title: Reviewing a plain code diff instead of artifacts
whenBad.why: /artifact shows artifacts (plans, diagrams, media files, code files pending approval), not a continuous line diff across turns and commits.
whenBad.alternative: /diff — Interactive Diff Viewer for changes, turns, and commits

commands.name: /btw
commands.summary: Asks a side question in the background without interrupting the main conversation.
commands.what: /btw belongs to the Utilities category. It fires off an extra question as a background task while the running main conversation continues undisturbed — handy for short side questions that shouldn't eat into the main thread's current context.

whenGood.title: Ask a quick side question without interrupting the main task
whenGood.example: /btw what does this function in utils.py do?

whenBad.title: The question is actually part of the main task
whenBad.why: /btw runs separately from the main thread in the background — not suited for questions meant to shape how the main task continues.
whenBad.alternative: Ask the question directly in the main prompt

commands.name: /clear
commands.summary: Clears the terminal and active conversation contexts. Alias: /new.
commands.what: /clear belongs to the Utilities category, alias /new. It resets both the terminal display and the active conversation contexts — for a clean restart within the same session.

whenGood.title: Start a new topic within the same session
whenGood.example: /clear after finishing a task, before starting a completely new topic

whenBad.title: You want to keep the current conversation and come back to it later
whenBad.why: /clear wipes the active context — mid-task you lose the thread's working state.
whenBad.alternative: Use /resume to switch between threads instead of clearing

commands.name: /config
commands.summary: Opens the interactive settings editor. Alias: /settings.
commands.what:
`/config` (alias `/settings`) belongs to the "Configurations" category according to the official reference table and opens the interactive settings editor overlay directly in the prompt box. You navigate through the options with the arrow keys, Enter changes values or opens an input field, Esc saves and closes the overlay.

This controls display and rendering options (alt-screen mode, color scheme, animation speed, verbosity), security and permission settings (approval levels for terminal commands, review requirement for written files, sandbox restrictions), as well as editor and system options such as the default text editor, desktop notifications, and telemetry. The values end up in the same settings.json as with manual editing – according to the docs, the CLI only writes values that deviate from the system default (sparse persistence). Individual startup flags can temporarily override settings; the overlay marks overridden values with a warning.

whenGood.title: Change CLI settings without manually editing settings.json
whenGood.example: Open /config and adjust, for example, the color scheme or the approval level for terminal commands directly in the panel

whenGood.title: Check whether a startup flag is currently temporarily overriding a setting
whenGood.example: Open /config — values overridden by a flag are marked with a warning in the overlay

whenBad.title: Only switching the reasoning model
whenBad.why: /config covers the entire configuration; there's a dedicated, more direct command for pure model selection.
whenBad.alternative: Use /model to choose the preferred reasoning model

commands.name: /context
commands.summary: Opens the context usage visualization.
commands.what:
/context belongs to the Utilities category and opens a panel that visually shows how much of the current session's available context window is already used — like the other utility commands, it can be called at any time, regardless of which panel or overlay is currently focused.

The display helps you judge when a long conversation is approaching its limits, for example before starting another large task or adding many files via `/add-dir`. When space runs low, other utility commands can help: `/clear` for a completely fresh session, or `/rewind` or `/undo` to jump back to a specific point in the conversation history instead of blindly continuing with a full context window.

For /context itself, the official docs currently only document the short description from the command reference; there's no dedicated detail page or changelog entries for it.

whenGood.title: Check remaining context capacity before a long task
whenGood.example: Call /context to see how much space is still free in the context window

whenGood.title: Decide whether a restart or rewind makes sense
whenGood.example: Check /context and, if the context window is running low, either restart fresh with /clear or jump back to an earlier point in the history with /rewind.

whenBad.title: Checking model quota (requests per time period) instead of the context window
whenBad.why: /context shows context-window usage, not the model's usage quota.
whenBad.alternative: /usage

commands.name: /copy
commands.summary: Copies the last agent response to the clipboard.
commands.what:
/copy belongs to the Utilities category and by default copies the agent's last response to the system clipboard — useful for pasting an explanation, code block, or summary directly into another application without manually selecting it.

Since version 1.1.6, the command also accepts an optional index argument: `/copy <n>` copies not the last response but the n-th-to-last response from the conversation history. This lets you grab an older response directly, without first scrolling back through the history or searching for it afterward.

/copy copies plain response text, not a structured code change with file and line references across multiple turns — that's what the Interactive Diff Viewer (`/diff`) is for, which shows and lets you navigate changes, turns, and commits separately.

whenGood.title: Copy the last response into a note
whenGood.example: /copy after a code explanation, to paste it into a note.

whenGood.title: Copy a specific older response
whenGood.example: /copy 3 copies not the last but the third-to-last response from the agent to the clipboard.

whenBad.title: Copying an entire code diff instead of plain text response
whenBad.why: /copy copies the text response, not a structured code diff across multiple files and turns.
whenBad.alternative: Open /diff and view the changes there

commands.name: /credits
commands.summary: Shows remaining G1 credits and purchase links.
commands.what:
`/credits` belongs to the "Account" category and, according to the official reference, opens the dedicated credits panel: it shows remaining G1 credits and purchase links as well as detailed usage statistics. G1 credits are personal AI premium credits that step in as fallback billing once the plan quota is used up. Via the `useG1Credits` setting in settings.json (toggleable via /config), you determine whether the CLI automatically falls back to your personal credit balance when the quota is exhausted, or blocks fallback billing.

The panel also offers direct links to buy more credits or upgrade the subscription. This clearly distinguishes /credits from `/usage` (alias `/quota`): /usage shows the model-specific API quota of your plan, while /credits shows the separate G1 balance that can be topped up with money – two different billing systems within the same CLI.

whenGood.title: Check the remaining balance before a bigger task
whenGood.example: Call /credits before starting a compute-intensive session, to see whether G1 fallback will be needed

whenGood.title: Trigger a top-up or subscription upgrade directly from the CLI
whenGood.example: Open /credits and use the purchase link in the panel, instead of manually searching for the billing page in the browser

whenBad.title: Checking the model-specific plan quota instead of the credit balance
whenBad.why: /credits only shows the G1 credits balance, not the consumption of the model quota included in the plan.
whenBad.alternative: Use /usage (alias /quota)

commands.name: /diff
commands.summary: Opens the interactive diff viewer with three modes (VCS/Turn/Commit).
commands.what: /diff belongs to the Utilities category. Tab, ← or → cycle through VCS, Turn, and Commit mode; c adds a comment on the current line, d deletes it, n/N jump between hunks, and Shift+Y sends the comments you've set to the agent while Shift+N discards them.

whenGood.title: Review the changes from a single turn
whenGood.example: Open /diff, switch to Turn mode with Tab, and check the latest change

whenGood.title: Send inline comments on individual hunks back to the agent
whenGood.example: Open /diff, add a comment to a line with c, and send it with Shift+Y

whenBad.title: You want an assessment of the changes, not just the raw diff text
whenBad.why: /diff only displays the diff text — it doesn't evaluate it.
whenBad.alternative: Ask the agent directly in the prompt to summarize or assess the changes

commands.name: /exit
commands.summary: Ends the TUI session and restores the host shell. Alias: /quit.
commands.what:
In the official Antigravity CLI reference, /exit belongs to the "Core" category and has the alias `/quit`. According to the docs it "closes the TUI session and restores your host shell" — so the command ends the running interactive terminal session and hands control back to the shell from which `agy` was started.

This makes /exit the regular way to leave an Antigravity CLI session, instead of hard-closing the terminal window or aborting the process with Ctrl+C. Because `/quit` as an alias has exactly the same function, it doesn't matter which of the two spellings you use — officially both are documented as equivalent.

Important: /exit only affects the current TUI session. According to the reference, the conversation history remains retrievable via /resume, provided the session wasn't cleared beforehand with /clear.

whenGood.title: Cleanly end the session and return to the host shell
whenGood.example: /exit, once the task is complete

whenGood.title: Use the alias if it's more familiar
whenGood.example: Type /quit — according to the docs, identical to /exit

whenBad.title: Only clear the context but keep working in the same session
whenBad.why: According to the docs, /exit ends the entire TUI session, not just the conversation context.
whenBad.alternative: Use /clear to start a new conversation within the same session

commands.name: /fast
commands.summary: Turns on fast mode, which skips reasoning plans for quick actions.
commands.what: According to the central slash command reference, /fast belongs to the Configurations category and enables a sped-up mode where the agent skips reasoning plans before acting, so it responds faster.

whenGood.title: Run a simple, clearly-defined action without lengthy planning
whenGood.example: Turn on /fast before requesting a simple file rename

whenBad.title: A complex task with several dependencies
whenBad.why: Without a reasoning plan, complex tasks carry a higher risk of incomplete or incorrect steps.
whenBad.alternative: Leave /fast off, or use /planning for multi-step tasks

commands.name: /feedback
commands.summary: Opens the feedback panel.
commands.what:
`/feedback` belongs to the "Utilities" category and, according to the official reference, opens the feedback submission panel – a form directly in the CLI through which you send feedback about using the Antigravity CLI to the Google team. The command is distinct from the separate `showFeedbackSurvey` setting in settings.json: this controls whether a short quality survey is automatically shown after completed tasks (default: on). /feedback, on the other hand, is the active way to report a concern that you can trigger yourself at any time, independent of this automatic survey – so you don't have to wait for the survey popup to give feedback.

The command serves purely to send feedback, not to fix problems in the running session: there's no response or solution within the CLI, the concern goes to the team as a message.

whenGood.title: Report a bug or improvement suggestion directly from the CLI
whenGood.example: Open /feedback and note the observation while the context is still fresh

whenGood.title: Give unsolicited feedback without waiting for the automatic survey
whenGood.example: Call /feedback yourself, instead of waiting for the showFeedbackSurvey popup after task completion

whenBad.title: A technical problem that needs to be solved immediately
whenBad.why: /feedback sends a message to the team, but doesn't provide a solution or answer within the running session.
whenBad.alternative: Consult /help or the troubleshooting docs

commands.name: /fork
commands.summary: Clones the current conversation thread into a parallel session. Alias: /branch.
commands.what: /fork belongs to the Conversations category, alias /branch. It duplicates the current thread, including context, into a new, parallel-running session, so different approaches can be pursued independently of each other.

whenGood.title: Try two approaches in parallel
whenGood.example: /fork to test an alternative implementation without losing the main thread

whenBad.title: You just want to go back to an earlier point in the same thread
whenBad.why: /fork creates a new parallel thread; it doesn't change the existing one.
whenBad.alternative: /rewind

commands.name: /help
commands.summary: Opens the help panel with commands and shortcuts.
commands.what:
/help belongs to the Utilities category and opens the help panel with an overview of all available slash commands and the active keyboard shortcuts, directly in the terminal.

The shortcuts tab is sorted by key combination, so you can look up which action sits behind which key without having to search the whole list. Since version 1.0.10, the panel also shows the path to the CLI log file — useful when you want to reproduce an error and need the associated logs for a bug report via `/feedback`.

/help doesn't replace a detailed explanation of individual features, though: it provides a compact reference of command names, short descriptions, and key combinations, not examples or background on how individual panels work.

whenGood.title: Look up available commands
whenGood.example: Call /help to see the list of all slash commands

whenGood.title: Find the log file for a bug report
whenGood.example: Open /help and copy the CLI log file path shown there, to include it via /feedback.

whenBad.title: Looking up detailed keyboard shortcuts for a single panel like /diff or /agents
whenBad.why: /help shows a general overview, not detailed keyboard shortcuts for individual panels.
whenBad.alternative: Open the respective panel itself, e.g. /diff or /agents

commands.name: /hooks
commands.summary: Browses the active pre-/post-hooks.
commands.what:
`/hooks` belongs, according to the official CLI reference, to the "Tools & Tasks" category and opens a searchable overview in the TUI of all currently loaded and active pre- and post-hooks. These are scripts that Antigravity automatically runs before or after certain agent actions, such as a pre-flight check before a tool call or automatic formatting after a file has been written.

Hooks are defined either directly in your `settings.json` or shipped as part of a plugin via its own `hooks.json`; `/hooks` shows you, bundled together, what is actively loaded from both sources. The underlying configuration lives by default at `~/.gemini/config/hooks.json` — an earlier bug, fixed in version 1.0.8, accidentally wrote changes to a different, non-shared path.

The command itself changes nothing: it is a pure inspection tool, not an editor for hooks.

whenGood.title: Check active hooks before a session
whenGood.example: Type /hooks to see whether a plugin has registered, for example, a post-edit formatting hook

whenGood.title: Find the cause of unexpected behavior
whenGood.example: After a surprising automatic format run following a save, open /hooks to check which hook is responsible

whenBad.title: Wanting to enable/disable a plugin entirely
whenBad.why: /hooks only shows an overview, it does not manage plugins directly.
whenBad.alternative: Use agy plugin enable <name> or agy plugin disable <name>

whenBad.title: Wanting to edit hooks yourself
whenBad.why: According to the docs, /hooks is a pure inspection tool, not an editor for hooks.json.
whenBad.alternative: Edit hooks.json directly in settings.json or in the respective plugin folder

commands.name: /keybindings
commands.summary: Opens the interactive keybinding editor.
commands.what:
/keybindings belongs to the "Configurations" category and, according to the official reference, opens "the interactive Keyboard Shortcut Editor" — that is, an interactive editor inside the TUI where you can customize Antigravity CLI keyboard shortcuts.

The "Using AGY CLI" docs page adds that the shortcuts can be edited either via this editor or directly in a JSON file. According to the official documentation, the file is located at `~/.gemini/antigravity-cli/keybindings.json`. To reset to the default configuration, according to the docs it's enough to delete this file.

/keybindings is therefore suited both for one-off adjustments via the interface and for version-controllable, manual editing of the JSON file — for example, to sync your own keyboard shortcut set across multiple machines.

whenGood.title: Change a keyboard shortcut that conflicts with another application
whenGood.example: Open /keybindings and reassign the affected shortcut in the interactive editor

whenGood.title: Sync your own keybindings across multiple machines
whenGood.example: Edit or copy the file ~/.gemini/antigravity-cli/keybindings.json directly, instead of opening the editor every time

whenBad.title: Change general settings instead of keyboard shortcuts
whenBad.why: According to the docs, /keybindings only covers keyboard shortcuts, not the rest of the configuration.
whenBad.alternative: Use /config or /settings

commands.name: /logout
commands.summary: Disconnects the profile and deletes the auth token from the keyring.
commands.what: /logout belongs to the Account category and signs out the connected Google account by removing the stored auth token from the OS keyring (Keychain/Secret Service/Credential Manager). The next start requires a fresh browser or URL+code auth flow.

whenGood.title: Switch accounts
whenGood.example: /logout, then restart agy and sign in with a different Google account

whenBad.title: You just want to end the current session, keeping the account connected
whenBad.why: /logout removes the auth token entirely; for a plain end of session a simple session exit is enough.
whenBad.alternative: /exit

commands.name: /mcp
commands.summary: Opens the MCP server manager.
commands.what: /mcp belongs to the Tools & Tasks category and opens a panel for managing connected MCP servers (stdio and remote via serverUrl), including connection status. Configuration lives separately in a global file (~/.gemini/config/mcp_config.json) and a workspace file (.agents/mcp_config.json).

whenGood.title: Check connected MCP servers and their status
whenGood.example: Open /mcp to see whether a server is connected

whenBad.title: You want to set a permission for a single MCP tool
whenBad.why: /mcp manages server connections; the granular mcp(server/tool) rules are handled through permissions management.
whenBad.alternative: /permissions

commands.name: /model
commands.summary: Picks the reasoning model, persisting across sessions.
commands.what: /model belongs to the Configurations category. The choice applies beyond the current session until changed again. Complements the --model startup flag and the agy models subcommand, which lists available models from the Shared Agent Engine (including Gemini 3.1 Pro/3.5 Flash on all plans, and Claude Sonnet/Opus 4.6 plus GPT-OSS-120b on Google AI Ultra only).

whenGood.title: Pick a stronger reasoning model for a more demanding task
whenGood.example: Open /model and switch to a more capable model

whenBad.title: You only want the model set for the next start, not permanently
whenBad.why: /model changes the choice persistently across sessions.
whenBad.alternative: Use agy --model <name> at startup

commands.name: /open
commands.summary: Opens a path in the system default editor.
commands.what:
/open belongs to the Utilities category and forces a given path to open in the default editor configured on your system — outside the CLI, in your familiar environment with syntax highlighting, search, and all the editor features the plain terminal view doesn't offer.

While typing, the command has supported shell-like path autocompletion since version 1.0.6, just like `/add-dir` — so you don't need to know the full filename by heart, but can complete it step by step.

/open is the right choice when you want to keep editing a file manually or read through it at leisure, instead of only seeing it as a snippet in the terminal. If you just want to give the agent a file as context in the prompt without opening it separately, the `@<path>` reference in the prompt is the more direct route.

whenGood.title: Open a file for manual editing outside the CLI
whenGood.example: /open src/index.ts

whenGood.title: Find a path via autocompletion
whenGood.example: Type /open src/ and complete it step by step through the directory structure until you reach the file you want.

whenBad.title: Just inserting a file path into the prompt
whenBad.why: /open launches the external editor, which isn't needed for a plain prompt reference.
whenBad.alternative: Use @<path> in the prompt

commands.name: /permissions
commands.summary: Opens the interactive tool permissions manager.
commands.what: /permissions belongs to the Configurations category. A scope picker lets you choose between Project, Shared, and Global, then between the rule viewer tabs allow/deny/ask; a adds a rule, e or Ctrl+G edits it, d or Backspace deletes it. Rules follow the format action(target), e.g. command(git) or mcp(server/tool).

whenGood.title: Allow specific commands to run automatically
whenGood.example: Open /permissions, pick the Project scope, and set command(git) to allow

whenGood.title: Block a specific MCP tool
whenGood.example: Open /permissions and set mcp(server/tool) to deny

whenBad.title: You want to bypass permissions entirely for a single start
whenBad.why: /permissions manages persistent rules, not a one-time skip for a single start.
whenBad.alternative: agy --dangerously-skip-permissions at startup (use with caution)

commands.name: /planning
commands.summary: Command removed since 1.1.0 per changelog/modes page, replaced by /plan prefix
commands.what:
`/planning` was originally a slash command from the "Configurations" category that activated a mode in which the agent first drafts a plan across multiple turns before executing, instead of acting directly — intended for complex engineering tasks with many dependencies.

Important: according to the dedicated Antigravity CLI page on execution modes as well as the official changelog, `/planning` (together with the old `/fast`) was removed in version 1.1.0 as a "vestigial command". It was replaced by a unified mode system: either you press `Shift+Tab` to cycle between the modes `default`, `accept-edits`, and `plan`, or you prefix your prompt with `/plan` so the CLI automatically switches to plan mode.

Note: the general command reference page still lists `/planning` as an active command with the same old description — this contradicts the dedicated modes page and the changelog and looks like an outdated piece of documentation.

whenGood.title: Have a multi-step task planned
whenGood.example: Prefix your prompt with /plan before a larger refactoring task (successor to the old /planning)

whenGood.title: Switch between execution modes
whenGood.example: Cycle between default, accept-edits, and plan with Shift+Tab, instead of typing the removed /planning

whenBad.title: Typing /planning like before
whenBad.why: According to the modes page and changelog, the command has been treated as a removed legacy command since version 1.1.0.
whenBad.alternative: Prefix the prompt with /plan or switch modes with Shift+Tab

whenBad.title: Having a trivial single action planned
whenBad.why: According to the modes page, planning overhead isn't worth it for trivial actions like typo fixes.
whenBad.alternative: Choose fast mode via Shift+Tab (the old /fast was also removed in 1.1.0 per the changelog)

commands.name: /rename
commands.summary: Renames the current session thread.
commands.what: /rename belongs to the Conversations category and assigns a new name to the current conversation thread, making it easier to find again later in the conversation picker.

whenGood.title: Give a thread a clear name before switching to a different topic
whenGood.example: /rename Migration-Auth-Refactor

whenBad.title: You want to rename a saved thread without it being active right now
whenBad.why: /rename acts on the currently active thread; saved threads have a rename option inside the resume picker.
whenBad.alternative: Open /resume and rename it there with F2

commands.name: /resume
commands.summary: Opens the conversation picker to load earlier threads. Aliases: /switch, /conversation.
commands.what: /resume belongs to the Conversations category, aliases /switch and /conversation. In the picker, F2 renames the selected thread, Ctrl+Delete deletes it, and Tab switches between the CLI tab and the Antigravity 2.0 tab to import running desktop conversations from the GUI. Complements the -c/--continue and --conversation <id> startup flags.

whenGood.title: Return to an earlier thread
whenGood.example: Open /resume and pick an earlier thread from the list

whenGood.title: Import a conversation started in Antigravity 2.0 (desktop GUI) into the CLI
whenGood.example: Open /resume and switch to the Antigravity tab with Tab

whenBad.title: You just want to continue the last conversation directly at startup, without a picker
whenBad.why: /resume opens an interactive panel; for a direct restart without picking, the startup flag is enough.
whenBad.alternative: agy -c / --continue at startup

commands.name: /rewind
commands.summary: Rolls the conversation history back to a previous checkpoint. Alias: /undo.
commands.what:
`/rewind` (alias `/undo`) belongs to the "Conversations" category and resets your current conversation thread to an earlier, stable state. According to the best-practices docs, the typical use case is: if an agent has made several changes in a row that cause build errors, you don't need to discard the session – you type /rewind (or /undo) to return to the last working checkpoint. The history after that point is overwritten, not kept in parallel.

This clearly distinguishes the command from `/fork` (alias `/branch`): fork clones the current session at a stable point into a parallel session, to test risky changes there without losing the main history – if the attempt fails, `/resume` takes you back to the main branch. /rewind is a genuine backward move within the same thread, not a branch.

whenGood.title: Undo several consecutive faulty changes by the agent
whenGood.example: /rewind after the agent has made three edits that break the build — back to the last stable state

whenGood.title: Rescue a session instead of restarting completely
whenGood.example: /undo right after a botched change, instead of discarding the conversation and starting over

whenBad.title: Trying an alternative approach in parallel to the existing history
whenBad.why: /rewind overwrites the history from the chosen point onward, instead of keeping it as a branch.
whenBad.alternative: Use /fork (alias /branch) to start a parallel session from the stable state, and return with /resume if unsuccessful

commands.name: /skills
commands.summary: Browses loaded local and global Agent Skills.
commands.what: /skills belongs to the Tools & Tasks category and shows the currently loaded skills from the workspace (.agents/skills/*.md) and the global directory (~/.gemini/antigravity-cli/skills/). Every markdown skill file automatically becomes its own /<skill-name> command.

whenGood.title: Check which skills are currently available
whenGood.example: Open /skills to see whether a newly added skill file was picked up

whenBad.title: You want to fully install or uninstall a plugin

commands.what: /statusline belongs to the Configurations category. Without an argument it toggles the statusline on/off; on/enable turns it on, off/disable turns it off, a passed shell command sets a custom renderer, reset resets the statusline, and help shows the options.

commands.name: /tasks
commands.summary: Opens the task manager panel for monitoring background shell logs.
commands.what:
According to the official Antigravity CLI reference, /tasks belongs to the "Tools & Tasks" category. The command "opens the Task Manager Panel to monitor background shell execution logs" — so it opens a dedicated panel showing running and completed background shell processes along with their logs.

This is relevant as soon as an agent starts a longer-running terminal command (such as a build or test run) in the background: instead of waiting, you can use /tasks to check the progress and output while the agent keeps working in parallel. According to the official CLI changelog, the list and detail view of /tasks was revised in an earlier version (start times on the left, status right-aligned), which suggests a tabular layout.

/tasks shows only shell task logs — according to the reference, a separate panel is provided for the status of subagents.

whenGood.example: Open /tasks while a build is running in the background to see the current output

whenGood.title: Get an overview of all active background processes
whenGood.example: Call /tasks to see which background shells are currently running or already finished

whenBad.title: Monitor subagent status instead of background shell tasks
whenBad.why: According to the reference, /tasks shows shell task logs; a separate panel is documented for subagents.

commands.name: /title
commands.summary: Toggles terminal window title updates.
commands.what:
/title belongs to the "Configurations" category and controls whether your terminal emulator's window title updates automatically. According to the dedicated docs page, when the feature is enabled, the title updates dynamically and shows the active model, the workspace, and the agent status.

The syntax is `/title [on|off]`: without an argument, the command toggles the current state; with `on` you explicitly turn title updates on, with `off` explicitly off. In the CLI reference, the short description is given as "toggle or set terminal window title updates".

This is useful, for example, when you have multiple terminal tabs or windows open with different Antigravity sessions and want to immediately tell from the window title which model or workspace is currently active, without first clicking into the respective window.

whenGood.title: Keep multiple terminal windows with different sessions apart
whenGood.example: /title on, so the window title shows the model and workspace of the respective session

whenGood.title: Deliberately turn off window title updates, e.g. because of your own title script
whenGood.example: /title off

whenBad.title: Customize the content of the status bar inside the TUI
whenBad.why: According to the docs, /title only affects the window title of the terminal emulator, not the status bar inside the TUI itself.
whenBad.alternative: Use /statusline

commands.name: /usage
commands.summary: Shows model quota usage. Alias: /quota.
commands.what:
/usage belongs to the Utilities category, has the alias `/quota`, and opens an interactive panel that shows your model quota usage: a breakdown of your usage limits and the remaining requests or tokens per supported model on your current plan.

On opening, the CLI forces a fresh sync of the quota values, both locally on disk and with the backend service — so you see the current state rather than a cached, outdated number. Navigate with the arrow keys or vim-style with `j`/`k`; `g`/`G` jumps to the start or end of the list; `Esc` or `q` closes the panel again.

This clearly distinguishes /usage from `/context`: this is about your request quota over time, not the current session's context-window usage.

whenGood.title: Check remaining requests in the current time window
whenGood.example: Call /usage before kicking off a large number of requests

whenGood.title: See the current instead of a cached quota state
whenGood.example: Open /usage or /quota to get a freshly synced state of the model quotas from the backend, instead of just a locally cached number.

whenBad.title: Checking G1 credits balance instead of general model quota
whenBad.why: /usage shows the plan quota; there's a separate command for the separate credits balance.
whenBad.alternative: /credits

commands.name: /bug
commands.summary: Reports a bug or shares your conversation.
commands.what:
Reports a bug or shares your conversation.

You choose how much session history to include and confirm on a consent screen first. Signed in to Anthropic on a first-party connection, the report goes to Anthropic; on a third-party provider or without Anthropic credentials, Claude Code writes it to a local archive under ~/.claude/feedback-bundles/ that you forward yourself. Alias: /share. Before v2.1.212, /bug and /share were aliases of /feedback.

whenGood.title: Report a bug with context to Anthropic
whenGood.example: /bug

whenGood.title: Without an Anthropic login: write the report locally and forward it yourself
whenGood.example: /bug report

whenBad.title: Not a bug but a product idea or general feedback
whenBad.why: /bug is built for bug reports and sharing a session.
whenBad.alternative: /feedback

commands.name: /stop
commands.summary: Stops the current background session.
commands.what:
Stops the running background session for good — the process is terminated, but not deleted afterward.

The command is only available while you're attached to a background session; the transcript and any worktree are preserved. If you only want to detach without ending the session, use /exit or press ← on an empty prompt. Outside the attached session, you instead stop it via Ctrl+X in the agent view or with claude stop <id> in the terminal (alias: claude kill). A stopped session can be restarted with an intact conversation using claude respawn <id>; to remove it completely, including the worktree, use claude rm <id>.

whenGood.title: End a background session that's no longer needed
whenGood.example: /stop, while attached to a background session — the transcript and worktree are preserved.

whenGood.title: Clean up after a completed background task
whenGood.example: /stop, after the background agent has finished its task, to free up resources; with claude respawn <id> it can be started again later if needed.

whenBad.title: Only detach, but keep the session running
whenBad.why: According to the docs, /stop ends the session for good; the log and worktree are preserved, but the work doesn't continue.
whenBad.alternative: /exit or ← on an empty prompt

whenBad.title: Not (or no longer) attached to the session
whenBad.why: According to the docs, /stop is only available while you're attached to a background session.
whenBad.alternative: Outside the session: press Ctrl+X in the agent view or run claude stop <id> in the terminal

commands.name: /team-onboarding
commands.summary: Generates a team onboarding guide from your usage history.
commands.what:
/team-onboarding analyzes your Claude Code usage from the last 30 days — sessions, commands used, and connected MCP servers — and automatically generates a Markdown guide from it. A teammate can simply paste this text as the first message in a new session and is immediately familiar with your typical setup: which tools, skills, and servers you use and how you normally work. The command needs no argument and only evaluates your own, local history.

If you're a claude.ai subscriber on a Pro, Max, Team, or Enterprise plan, `/team-onboarding` additionally provides a share link that colleagues can open directly in Claude Code, without having to manually copy the generated text. Without such a subscription, only the local Markdown file is created.

whenGood.title: Onboard new team members
whenGood.example: After a few weeks of active project work, run /team-onboarding so a new team member can use your setup as their first message

whenGood.title: Share your own setup as a link
whenGood.example: With a claude.ai subscription (Pro/Max/Team/Enterprise), send the generated share link directly to colleagues so they can open it in Claude Code without copy-paste

whenBad.title: Fresh project with no usage history of your own
whenBad.why: The guide is built from your sessions, commands, and MCP server usage over the last 30 days; without history, it stays thin or empty.
whenBad.alternative: Use `/init` for a project-based CLAUDE.md

commands.name: /terminal-setup
commands.summary: Configures terminal keybindings such as Shift+Enter.
commands.what:
Sets up several terminal settings in one step, most importantly Shift+Enter for a line break instead of sending. The command is only needed in VS Code, Cursor, Devin Desktop, Alacritty, and Zed — other terminals like Ghostty, Kitty, iTerm2, WezTerm, Warp, Apple Terminal, or Windows Terminal already support Shift+Enter without setup. In gnome-terminal and JetBrains IDEs, the command is missing entirely; there, Ctrl+J or backslash followed by Enter helps instead.

Depending on the terminal, the command does more than just assign keys: in VS Code, Cursor, and Devin Desktop it additionally disables GPU acceleration and adjusts the mouse wheel sensitivity for fullscreen mode. In Apple Terminal it activates Option as the Meta key and the audible bell; in iTerm2 it lets /copy access the system clipboard.

whenGood.title: Activate Shift+Enter in the VS Code or Cursor terminal
whenGood.example: /terminal-setup

whenGood.title: Unlock clipboard access for /copy in iTerm2
whenGood.example: run /terminal-setup once in iTerm2, after that /copy can write text to the system clipboard.

whenBad.title: A terminal that already supports the shortcuts out of the box
whenBad.why: According to the docs, terminals like Ghostty, Kitty, iTerm2, WezTerm, Warp, Apple Terminal, or Windows Terminal already support Shift+Enter without setup.
whenBad.alternative: do nothing — the shortcuts already work

whenBad.title: gnome-terminal or a JetBrains IDE (PyCharm, Android Studio, …)
whenBad.why: According to the docs, Shift+Enter is technically unavailable there, /terminal-setup doesn't help there.
whenBad.alternative: use Ctrl+J or backslash followed by Enter for a line break

commands.name: /theme
commands.summary: Changes the color theme.
commands.what:
Changes the color theme.

Includes an auto option that matches your terminal’s light or dark background, light and dark variants, colorblind-accessible (daltonized) themes, ANSI themes that use your terminal’s color palette, and any custom themes from ~/.claude/themes/ or plugins. Select "New custom theme…" to create one.

whenGood.title: Switch to a light or dark theme
whenGood.example: /theme

whenGood.title: Pick a colorblind-accessible theme
whenGood.example: /theme

whenBad.title: Change the terminal font or size
whenBad.why: /theme only controls Claude Code’s colors, not the terminal’s own rendering.
whenBad.alternative: use your terminal app’s settings

commands.name: /tui
commands.summary: Sets the terminal renderer and relaunches into it.
commands.what:
`/tui` determines which renderer draws the interface and restarts Claude Code with the conversation history preserved. `/tui fullscreen` switches to the flicker-free alt-screen renderer (like `vim` or `htop`): it reduces the amount of data sent to the terminal, keeps memory usage constant during long conversations, and brings mouse support (clicking, dragging to select, scrolling with the mouse wheel) as well as a fixed input area at the bottom of the screen. `/tui default` switches back to the classic renderer, which keeps the conversation in the terminal's native scrollback, so that, for example, Cmd+F search and tmux copy mode continue to work directly. Without an argument, `/tui` only reports which renderer is currently active, without changing anything.

According to the docs, fullscreen rendering is a research preview: it has been tested on common terminal emulators, but may still show rendering glitches on rarer terminals or configurations. Alternatively, the same mode can be enabled permanently at startup via the environment variable `CLAUDE_CODE_NO_FLICKER=1`.

whenGood.title: Fix flickering or scroll jumps in the VS Code terminal or tmux
whenGood.example: Run /tui fullscreen if the screen flickers while streaming tool output or the scroll position keeps jumping back to the top.

whenGood.title: Check which renderer is currently active
whenGood.example: Type /tui without an argument to check whether the current session is running in the classic or the fullscreen renderer.

whenBad.title: Expecting the conversation history to be lost or reset in the process
whenBad.why: According to the docs, switching keeps the history and only restarts the renderer; the command doesn't perform a reset.
whenBad.alternative: Use /clear to actually clear the history.

whenBad.title: Wanting to use native terminal search (Cmd+F) or tmux copy mode directly for the conversation
whenBad.why: In the fullscreen renderer, the conversation sits in the alternate screen buffer instead of the native scrollback — Cmd+F and tmux search find nothing there.
whenBad.alternative: Switch to transcript mode with Ctrl+O and press [ there to write the conversation into the native scrollback, or use /tui default.

commands.name: /ultrareview
commands.summary: Runs a deep, multi-agent code review in a cloud sandbox.
commands.what:
Runs a deep, multi-agent code review in a cloud sandbox.

Pass a PR reference to review that pull request, or a branch name to change the comparison base. The preferred invocation is now /code-review ultra, and /ultrareview remains as an alias. Includes 3 free runs on Pro and Max, then requires usage credits.

commands.summary: Configures usage credits or requests them from your admin.
commands.what:
Configures usage credits, or requests them from your admin, when you hit a limit.

On Pro and Max plans, opens an in-CLI dialog to buy usage credits, set a monthly spend limit, and configure auto-reload. On Claude Code versions before v2.1.207 and on other plans, it opens the usage-credits billing page in your browser instead. Team and Enterprise members without billing access send a usage-credits request to their admin after confirming in a dialog.

whenGood.title: Buy more credits after hitting the limit (Pro/Max)
whenGood.example: /usage-credits

whenGood.title: Without billing access, request credits from your admin
