commands.name: /voice
commands.summary: Toggles voice dictation on or off.
commands.what:
Turns voice dictation on or off, or directly activates a specific mode: /voice hold holds down a key while speaking (default mode), /voice tap starts and stops the recording by tapping, /voice off deactivates it. Without an argument, the command just toggles between on and off and keeps the mode last used.

A Claude.ai account is required — voice dictation doesn't work with a plain API key, Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud, or Microsoft Foundry. A local microphone is also needed; in remote environments like Claude Code on the web or over SSH, the feature isn't available. Transcription doesn't consume any messages or tokens and doesn't count toward the limit in /usage.

whenGood.title: Speak into the terminal instead of typing
whenGood.example: /voice tap — tap the space bar once, speak, tap again; from three words on it's sent automatically.

whenGood.title: Only dictate while a key is held down
whenGood.example: /voice hold — hold the space bar, speak, releasing it inserts the text at the cursor position and waits for Enter.

whenBad.title: Remote session or Claude Code on the web
whenBad.why: According to the docs, voice dictation needs a local microphone and doesn't work in remote environments like Claude Code on the web or SSH sessions.
whenBad.alternative: keep typing on the keyboard

whenBad.title: Only API key, Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud, or Microsoft Foundry without a Claude.ai account
whenBad.why: According to the docs, the speech-to-text service is only available with a Claude.ai account, not with a direct Anthropic API key, Bedrock, Vertex, or Foundry configuration.
whenBad.alternative: connect a Claude.ai account with /login, or keep typing on the keyboard

commands.name: /web-setup
commands.summary: Connects your GitHub account to Claude Code on the web.
commands.what:
`/web-setup` connects your GitHub account to Claude Code on the web — using the local credentials of your installed `gh` CLI, not via its own OAuth flow. The reference doesn't mention further arguments or flags.

The command is also triggered automatically: if you set up a recurring cloud routine with `/schedule`, Claude Code independently asks for this connection if GitHub isn't linked yet. In addition, `/web-setup` now warns before replacing an existing GitHub App connection instead of silently overwriting an old link.

A prerequisite is an installed and signed-in `gh` CLI; without it, the command can't read credentials or establish a connection.

whenGood.title: Link GitHub with Claude Code on the web
whenGood.example: Call `/web-setup` to give Claude Code on the web access to your own repos.

whenGood.title: Set up before a cloud routine
whenGood.example: Run `/web-setup` once before `/schedule` so the routine can access GitHub directly instead of asking for it mid-way through.

whenBad.title: Without an installed gh CLI
whenBad.why: The command uses the local credentials of the `gh` CLI; without it, it can't connect anything.
whenBad.alternative: First install the `gh` CLI and sign in with `gh auth login`.

whenBad.title: Replacing an existing connection
whenBad.why: The command does warn before replacing an existing GitHub App connection, but whoever dismisses the warning loses the old link.
whenBad.alternative: Read the warning carefully and cancel if unsure.

commands.name: /workflows
commands.summary: Opens the progress view for running workflows.
commands.what:
`/workflows` opens the progress view for dynamic workflows: select, watch, pause, resume, stop, or save running and completed runs as your own command. A workflow runs in the background and distributes work across many subagents; the view opens immediately, even while a response is currently running.

In the view, according to the doc, these keys apply: `p` pauses or resumes the run, `x` stops the selected agent or — when the run itself is focused — the whole workflow, `r` restarts a running agent, `s` saves the script as its own command, project-wide under `.claude/workflows/` or personally under `~/.claude/workflows/`.

A paused run can be resumed: finished agents deliver their cached result, the rest continues live. This only works within the same session, though — after a restart, the workflow starts over from scratch.

whenGood.title: Watch a running workflow
whenGood.example: Call `/workflows`, select the run with the arrow keys, and pause it with `p` to briefly do something else.

whenGood.title: Save a run as a command
whenGood.example: After a successful review workflow, open `/workflows`, select the run, and save it under `.claude/workflows/` with `s` to reuse it in the future.

whenBad.title: No workflow is running
whenBad.why: The view shows running and completed workflows; without one, it stays empty.
whenBad.alternative: First start a workflow, for example via a bundled workflow like `/deep-research`.

whenBad.title: Expecting resumption after a restart
whenBad.why: According to the doc, resuming only works within the same session; if Claude Code is closed while a workflow is running, the next session starts it over from scratch.
whenBad.alternative: Leave the session open, or deliberately restart the workflow.

commands.name: /pr-comments
commands.summary: No longer exists — removed in version 2.1.91.
commands.what:
No longer exists — removed in version 2.1.91.

Instead of a dedicated command, you now ask Claude directly to view a pull request’s comments. On earlier versions, /pr-comments fetched a GitHub pull request’s comments (auto-detecting the current branch’s PR, or taking a PR URL or number) and required the gh CLI.

whenGood.title: Nothing — the command is gone
whenGood.example: Ask Claude directly: "Look at the comments on PR 42."

whenBad.title: On version 2.1.91 or later
whenBad.why: the command was removed in 2.1.91 and does nothing.
whenBad.alternative: ask Claude directly for the PR comments

commands.name: /init
commands.summary: Generates an AGENTS.md scaffold for the current project.
commands.what:
`/init` generates an `AGENTS.md` scaffold for the current project or directory. `AGENTS.md` holds project-specific instructions and context that Codex automatically reads at every session — the counterpart to `CLAUDE.md` in Claude Code. According to the docs, the file captures persistent instructions for the repository or the subdirectory you're currently working in.

`/init` is documented both in the pure terminal CLI command list and in the general Codex command reference and works identically there — unlike `/worktree` or `/cloud`, it's therefore not a desktop-app-exclusive feature, but a regular terminal CLI command. The command only creates the basic scaffold; you have to add the actual content — project rules, coding conventions, test commands — yourself afterward or have Codex fill it in specifically.

whenGood.title: Set up a new project for Codex
whenGood.example: /init

whenGood.title: Have the project rules recaptured after a major structural change in the repo
whenGood.example: call /init, then manually add new test commands to the generated scaffold

whenBad.title: AGENTS.md already exists and is maintained
whenBad.why: /init creates a fresh scaffold and can overwrite existing, carefully maintained project notes.
whenBad.alternative: edit the existing AGENTS.md directly instead of having it regenerated

commands.name: /compact
commands.summary: Compacts the current chat’s context.
commands.what:
Summarizes the visible chat history to free up tokens in the context window. In the Codex CLI's source code, the purpose is literally named: "summarize conversation to prevent hitting the context limit" — so /compact is meant to proactively prevent the conversation from hitting the context limit.

According to the source code, the command can't be triggered while Codex is actively working on a task; you have to wait until the current turn is finished. Codex now also compresses the history automatically in the background once a token budget threshold is reached — according to release notes (including rust-v0.143.0 and rust-v0.145.0, July 2026), now with configurable fallback settings and session-start hooks around this automatic compression. `/compact` additionally gives you the option to trigger this proactively yourself before Codex does it on its own. The command appears both in the terminal CLI reference and in the general app composer overview.

whenGood.title: Free up space before a long task
whenGood.example: Call /compact before starting a new, extensive research task, so the existing history doesn't unnecessarily block context.

whenGood.title: Compress manually instead of waiting
whenGood.example: Enter /compact right after a long debugging section instead of waiting for automatic background compression.

whenBad.title: While Codex is still actively working
whenBad.why: According to the source code, /compact is one of the commands that isn't available while a task is running.
whenBad.alternative: wait for the current task to finish (or cancel it), then call /compact

whenBad.title: The conversation is still short
whenBad.why: Summarizing costs detail; as long as there's enough context window free, it doesn't help much.
whenBad.alternative: just keep working

commands.name: /reasoning
commands.summary: No standalone command in the Codex terminal CLI, see /model
commands.what:
According to the general Codex slash commands reference (there explicitly headed as a reference for the ChatGPT desktop app), `/reasoning` selects the reasoning effort for the current chat.

Important limitation for the terminal CLI: `/reasoning` does not appear in the CLI's own "Built-in slash commands" table on the reference page for the CLI interface, and no command with this name exists in the Codex CLI's open-source code (file slash_command.rs) either. There, `/model` takes over this task instead — according to the source code literally described as "choose what model and reasoning effort to use". The reasoning effort concept is generally real in Codex, though, and is actively being developed further: release notes from July 2026 mention new levels such as "Max" and "Ultra" in addition to the familiar ones. In the terminal CLI, you set the reasoning depth via `/model`, not via a standalone `/reasoning` command.

whenGood.title: Adjust reasoning depth in the desktop composer
whenGood.example: Call /reasoning to choose between more thoroughness and more speed for the current chat in the ChatGPT desktop app composer — documented there as a separate command.

whenGood.title: Same goal in the terminal CLI
whenGood.example: In the Codex terminal CLI, call /model instead, which according to the source code sets both model and reasoning effort together.

whenBad.title: Expecting the command in the terminal CLI
whenBad.why: /reasoning is missing both from the CLI reference table and from the Codex CLI's open-source code (no SlashCommand::Reasoning).
whenBad.alternative: use /model in the terminal CLI

whenBad.title: Only switching the model
whenBad.why: Where available, /reasoning only changes the reasoning effort, not the model itself.
whenBad.alternative: use /model to also switch the model

commands.name: /fast
commands.summary: Turns a Fast service tier on or off, when available.
commands.what:
`/fast` turns a so-called Fast service tier for the currently selected model on or off, provided the model catalog offers such a tier for that model at all. The Fast tier prioritizes response speed; whether it exists depends on the respective model and catalog, not on any manual configuration on your part. Your choice is remembered for the current session.

Unlike `/worktree` or `/cloud`, `/fast` is documented both in the pure terminal CLI command list and in the general Codex command reference — so it's a genuine terminal CLI feature, not a desktop-app-exclusive one. Despite the terse name, it's not an easter egg but an officially documented feature for model control, alongside `/model` (full model selection) and `/reasoning` (reasoning effort).

whenGood.title: Prefer faster responses when the current model offers a Fast tier
whenGood.example: /fast

whenGood.title: Check after switching models whether the Fast setting still makes sense
whenGood.example: switch /model, then call /fast again

whenBad.title: The current model doesn't offer a Fast tier
whenBad.why: According to the docs, /fast only has an effect if the model catalog provides a Fast tier for the selected model at all.
whenBad.alternative: choose a model with Fast support via /model

commands.name: /personality
commands.summary: Chooses how Codex responds, when the model supports personalities.
commands.what:
`/personality` chooses a communication style for Codex's responses, provided the currently used model supports personalities. This lets you make Codex sound more concise, more explanatory, or more collaborative, for example. According to the docs, the command only changes the tone and style of the responses — not your actual instructions and not the technical content of the work.

Like `/fast`, `/personality` is documented both in the pure terminal CLI command list and in the general Codex command reference, so it's a regular terminal CLI feature and not a desktop-app-exclusive one. Despite the unusual name, it's not an easter egg but an officially documented feature — whether it's available for your current model depends on the model itself, similar to `/fast`.

whenGood.title: Adjust the response style to your own working style, e.g. more concise instead of detailed
whenGood.example: /personality

whenGood.title: Check which styles are now available after switching models
whenGood.example: switch /model, then open /personality

whenBad.title: The current model doesn't support personalities
whenBad.why: According to the docs, /personality is only available if the model offers this feature.
whenBad.alternative: choose a model that supports personalities via /model

commands.name: /memories
commands.summary: Sets whether the chat may use or create memories, when Memories is available.
commands.what:
Determines whether the current chat may access memories (recollections across sessions) or generate new ones. The terminal CLI docs describe this literally as toggling "memory injection or memory generation", without leaving the terminal interface (TUI).

The feature depends on an availability condition: "if memories is available". According to Codex release notes (rust-v0.145.0 from 07/21/2026 — just a few days before this was written), the internal feature flag for memories was only recently stabilized there, alongside a paginated session history still marked as experimental. So the feature set is still being expanded, and older Codex versions may not know the command yet, or only in a limited form. According to the source code, `/memories` also can't be called while Codex is actively working on a task — you have to let the current turn finish before the command responds.

whenGood.title: Turn off memories for a sensitive chat
whenGood.example: Call /memories and disable creating new memories for this one chat before discussing confidential details.

whenGood.title: Quickly check whether memories is active
whenGood.example: Open /memories to check whether the current chat is currently using or generating memories, without leaving it for settings.

whenBad.title: Memories not available in the installed version
whenBad.why: According to release notes, the feature flag was only stabilized on 07/21/2026; older or restricted installations still lack the command.
whenBad.alternative: update Codex CLI or keep working without memories

whenBad.title: While Codex is still working on a task
whenBad.why: According to the source code, /memories is one of the commands locked while a task is running.
whenBad.alternative: wait for the running task to finish, then call /memories

commands.name: /ide
commands.summary: Turns IDE context on or off.
commands.what:
The name `/ide-context` comes from the general Codex command reference, which applies across all surfaces: there, the command turns shared IDE context on or off. In the pure terminal CLI's own documentation, the identical feature is instead called `/ide` (with optional arguments like `/ide on`, `/ide off`, or `/ide status`) and pulls open files, the current selection, and further editor context from a connected IDE extension into the next prompt.

It's the same feature under two different names in two different docs tables, not two separate features. It requires a running IDE with the Codex extension installed (e.g. VS Code), which supplies context via a local IPC connection. According to several issues reported in the Codex GitHub repository, activation occasionally fails even when the IDE extension is active.

whenGood.title: Have Codex automatically read along the IDE's open files and current selection
whenGood.example: /ide (in the terminal CLI; referred to as /ide-context in the general command reference)

whenGood.title: Specifically check or set whether IDE context is currently active
whenGood.example: /ide status or /ide on

whenBad.title: Codex runs without a connected IDE in the pure terminal
whenBad.why: Without an active IDE extension there's no IDE context that the command could turn on or off.
whenBad.alternative: reference files yourself specifically via mention

whenBad.title: You're looking for exactly the command name /ide-context in the terminal and can't find it
whenBad.why: The pure terminal CLI documents the same feature under the name /ide, not /ide-context.
whenBad.alternative: use /ide in the terminal

commands.name: /feedback
commands.summary: Opens the feedback dialog, optionally with logs.
commands.what:
`/feedback` opens the Codex CLI's feedback dialog. You type `/feedback` and confirm with Enter; Codex then walks you through several prompts and optionally lets you attach logs or diagnostic data, after which Codex submits this information to the Codex team.

According to the doc, the command is meant to send logs to the Codex maintainers — that is, to report specific problems or share diagnostics, not as a help channel for content questions during the running chat.

The command belongs to the standalone terminal CLI reference with its own doc section and step-by-step instructions; it also appears in the overarching command table with the same meaning.

whenGood.title: Report a bug with logs
whenGood.example: Codex behaves unexpectedly in a certain scenario, so you call `/feedback` and attach the logs for diagnosis.

whenGood.title: Submit a feature suggestion
whenGood.example: Send an idea for a missing feature directly to the maintainers via `/feedback`.

whenBad.title: It's a content question
whenBad.why: According to the doc, the command is intended for feedback to the maintainers, not as a help channel within the session.
whenBad.alternative: Ask the question directly in the chat.

commands.name: /approve
commands.summary: Approves one retry after an automatic-review denial.
commands.what:
`/approve` approves a retry for an action that the automatic reviewer previously rejected. According to the doc, the command only has an effect when Auto Review is active. Auto Review replaces manual approval at the sandbox boundary with a separate reviewer agent that approves or rejects requests such as risky shell commands, network access, or write access outside allowed paths.

When you call `/approve`, a list of the most recently rejected actions opens — Codex stores up to ten per task. You select one and approve it for exactly one retry.

The approval is tightly scoped: it applies only to exactly this action, not to similar future ones, and the new attempt still goes through Auto Review, which can reject it again.

whenGood.title: Retry an incorrectly blocked action
whenGood.example: The reviewer rejected a harmless lint command outside the allowed paths; you approve it via `/approve` for a retry.

whenGood.title: Steer specifically after a rejection
whenGood.example: Codex reports a rejection by Auto Review; via `/approve` you approve exactly this one action.

whenBad.title: Auto Review isn't active at all
whenBad.why: According to the doc, the command only applies to interactive approvals with Auto Review active; if the approval policy is set to "never", there's nothing to check.
whenBad.alternative: Adjust the approval policy via `/permissions` or the configuration.

whenBad.title: Wanting to permanently loosen the policy
whenBad.why: According to the doc, the command only approves a single retry for exactly one action, not a category of future actions.
whenBad.alternative: Adjust the Auto Review policy in `config.toml` or set tighter path rules.

commands.name: /side
commands.summary: Starts a temporary side chat without disturbing the main chat.
commands.what:
Starts an ephemeral side conversation without interrupting the main conversation. In the Codex CLI's open-source code, the command is literally described as "start a side conversation in an ephemeral fork"; `/btw` also works as an alias.

You can attach a message directly, e.g. `/side how do I export this as CSV?` — then the side conversation starts immediately with that content instead of opening an empty input first. Within an active side conversation, only a few additional commands are available according to the source code, such as `/copy`, `/diff`, `/status`, `/usage`, `/mention`, or `/ide` — most other slash commands remain reserved for the main conversation. According to Codex release rust-v0.145.0 (07/21/2026), a reliability bug was also fixed shortly before this was written: side conversations no longer incorrectly inherit turns, and a race condition at startup was removed. The command appears both in the terminal CLI table and in the general app composer overview.

whenGood.title: Split off a quick side question
whenGood.example: /side how do I export this table as CSV? — the answer doesn't end up in the main conversation.

whenGood.title: Start directly with content
whenGood.example: /side give me the syntax for a git rebase quickly, so I can keep working in the main conversation.

whenBad.title: The answer needs to land in the main conversation
whenBad.why: According to the source code, /side works in its own ephemeral fork, separate from the main conversation.
whenBad.alternative: ask the question directly in the main chat

whenBad.title: Additional slash commands are needed in the side conversation
whenBad.why: In the source code, only a small command list (including /copy, /diff, /status, /usage) is enabled for active side conversations.
whenBad.alternative: switch back to the main chat, where all commands are available

commands.name: /project
commands.summary: Chooses a project for new chats.
commands.what:
`/project` selects a project that new chats start with. The slash command reference describes it briefly as "Choose a project for new chats" — the selected project provides context such as files, instructions, and connected sources that newly started chats access.

Crucial for context: the doc on projects and chats makes clear that the ChatGPT Projects view is a feature of the ChatGPT desktop app, and states literally that the Codex CLI treats the directory you start it in as the project and doesn't show the Projects view at all.

In the terminal CLI, the project is therefore determined solely by the starting directory (or `--cd <directory>` respectively `-C`). The IDE extension accordingly uses the opened folder as the local project.

whenGood.title: Tie new chats to the same files
whenGood.example: You're working on a redesign for an extended period and select the matching project so new chats automatically use its files and instructions.

whenGood.title: Bundle multiple chats for the same effort
whenGood.example: Use a shared project for a feature with multiple subtasks, instead of starting each chat in isolation.

whenBad.title: Expected in the terminal CLI
whenBad.why: According to the doc, in the terminal CLI the starting directory already determines the project; the CLI doesn't show the ChatGPT Projects view at all.
whenBad.alternative: Start the terminal CLI in the desired directory, or set it explicitly with `--cd <directory>`.

whenBad.title: The work is a one-off
whenBad.why: According to the doc, a project isn't worth it for an isolated chat without recurring context needs.
whenBad.alternative: Start the chat without a project.

commands.name: /cloud
commands.summary: Runs the chat in the cloud (general Codex command reference).
commands.what:
`/cloud` runs the current chat in the cloud instead of locally, provided cloud execution is available — the work then runs on remote resources provided by OpenAI instead of on your machine. This is how the general Codex command reference describes it, which applies across all Codex surfaces.

Important: `/cloud` doesn't appear as an interactive slash command in the pure terminal CLI's own documentation. What the terminal CLI officially offers instead is the subcommand `codex cloud` (e.g. `codex cloud exec`, `codex cloud list`, `codex cloud apply <TASK_ID>`) — this lets you start, list, and take over cloud tasks directly via normal command-line syntax instead of via a chat slash command. For you as a pure terminal user, `codex cloud …` is the documented way; `/cloud` belongs more to the general, composer-related command set.

whenGood.title: Shift compute load from the local machine to the cloud, where /cloud is available as a slash command
whenGood.example: /cloud

whenGood.title: Start a cloud task or take over a result from the terminal CLI
whenGood.example: codex cloud exec --env ENV_ID "fix tests" or codex cloud apply <TASK_ID>

whenBad.title: You want to use it directly as a slash command in the pure terminal CLI
whenBad.why: According to the CLI-specific docs, /cloud isn't part of the terminal command list, but of the general Codex command reference.
whenBad.alternative: use the subcommand codex cloud (exec/list/apply/status/diff) in the terminal

whenBad.title: The task needs your local files directly
whenBad.why: In the cloud, the workspace isn't on your machine.
whenBad.alternative: /local or keep working locally in the terminal

commands.name: /local
commands.summary: Runs the chat in your local workspace.
commands.what:
`/local` sets a Codex chat to run in your local workspace instead of the cloud; the slash command reference describes it briefly as "Run the chat in your local workspace". Its counterpart is cloud execution, or selecting a specific environment.

Important for context: the doc on Codex environments explicitly describes this selection as a feature of the ChatGPT desktop app — you make it there when starting a new chat. Local and Worktree chats both run on your own machine with direct file access; only Cloud runs remotely in a container.

The standalone terminal CLI reference, on the other hand, doesn't list `/local` — the terminal CLI is fundamentally local anyway, with no dedicated switch command of its own.

whenGood.title: Keep direct file access
whenGood.example: You want to work with full access to your local files, so you stay local instead of moving the chat to the cloud.

whenGood.title: Fast iteration without cloud latency
whenGood.example: For a quick bugfix you want to test right away, you stay in the local workspace.

whenBad.title: The task should run independent of the machine
whenBad.why: Local execution ties the work to your machine; for remote execution you need a cloud environment.
whenBad.alternative: Switch to a configured cloud environment.

whenBad.title: Expecting the command in the terminal CLI
whenBad.why: According to the doc, the Local/Worktree/Cloud selection is made via the ChatGPT desktop app; the terminal CLI doesn't list `/local`.
whenBad.alternative: In the terminal, simply start `codex` in the desired directory — that's inherently local.

commands.name: /cloud-environment
commands.summary: Chooses the cloud environment for the chat.
commands.what:
`/cloud-environment` selects the cloud environment in which a Codex chat runs when you opt for cloud execution. According to the doc on Codex environments, you open the ChatGPT dropdown in the ChatGPT desktop app, select Codex, and choose between Local, Worktree, and Cloud when starting a new chat.

A cloud environment determines what Codex installs and runs during cloud chats: dependencies, tools like linters or formatters, environment variables. At startup, Codex checks out your branch or commit in a container, runs your setup script, and then continues working in the preinstalled default image `universal` if you're not using your own setup. Environments are configured in the Codex settings.

Important for context: the pure terminal CLI reference doesn't list this command — the doc explicitly describes the environment selection as a feature of the ChatGPT desktop app.

whenGood.title: Switch between cloud environments
whenGood.example: You've set up two environments with different Node versions and select the right one before the next cloud chat.

whenGood.title: Secure the toolchain before a cloud task
whenGood.example: Before starting a cloud chat with special dependencies, you check whether the environment with the matching preinstalled packages is active.

whenBad.title: The chat runs locally
whenBad.why: According to the doc, the command only determines which environment is used for cloud execution — it has no effect during local execution.
whenBad.alternative: First switch to the cloud via the Local/Worktree/Cloud selection.

whenBad.title: Expected in the pure terminal CLI
whenBad.why: The doc explicitly describes the Local/Worktree/Cloud selection as a feature of the ChatGPT desktop app; the terminal CLI reference doesn't list the command.
whenBad.alternative: In the terminal, use the `codex cloud` subcommand instead to start cloud tasks.

commands.name: /worktree
commands.summary: Starts the chat in a new Git worktree.
commands.what:
`/worktree` starts the current chat in a new Git worktree instead of in the normal working directory. A worktree is an additional working copy checked out from the same repository with its own branch — the agent's changes land there without touching your main branch. This way, multiple chats can work on the same project in parallel without interfering with each other; scheduled background tasks also run on their own worktrees according to the docs.

Important for you as a CLI user: according to the official docs, this worktree selection is only available in Codex within the ChatGPT desktop app (via the composer menu when starting a new chat), not in the pure terminal CLI. `/worktree` is listed in the general Codex command reference, but doesn't appear in the terminal CLI's own command list. In the pure terminal, `git worktree add` remains your manual option instead.

whenGood.title: Let multiple chats work on the same repo in parallel without getting in each other's way
whenGood.example: /worktree in the desktop app, while another chat keeps working on the main branch

whenGood.title: Try out a risky refactor in isolation before it touches the main branch
whenGood.example: /worktree, do the refactor in the new branch, only merge afterward

whenBad.title: You work exclusively in the terminal CLI
whenBad.why: According to the docs, worktrees are only available in Codex in the ChatGPT desktop app; the terminal CLI doesn't know /worktree as its own command.
whenBad.alternative: work manually with `git worktree add` or switch to the desktop app

whenBad.title: No Git repository present
whenBad.why: A worktree requires a Git repo.
whenBad.alternative: stay in the normal workspace

commands.name: /quit
commands.summary: Exits the session.
commands.what:
`/quit` immediately ends the running Codex CLI session. You type the command into the composer and confirm with Enter, upon which the session closes. According to the doc, `/quit` is functionally identical to `/exit` — both end the same session, `/exit` is just an alternative spelling. Alternatively, the session can also be closed with `Ctrl+C`.

The doc explicitly advises using the command only after you've saved or committed important changes: Codex ends immediately, without asking beforehand or saving automatically.

Unlike `/cloud-environment` or `/project`, for example, `/quit` is clearly documented with its own doc section as part of the pure terminal session.

whenGood.title: The work is finished
whenGood.example: After committing all your changes, type `/quit` to end the session cleanly.

whenGood.title: Controlled instead of a hard close
whenGood.example: Instead of force-closing the terminal window, use `/quit` so Codex ends the session in an orderly way.

whenBad.title: Changes aren't saved yet
whenBad.why: According to the doc, Codex ends the session immediately — unsaved work is lost.
whenBad.alternative: Commit or save first, then call `/quit` or `/exit`.

commands.name: /opus
commands.summary: Jumps straight to the Opus model family without opening the picker.
commands.what:
`/opus` is a model shortcut: it takes you straight to the Opus model family, without first opening the model picker via `/model` and clicking through it. According to the changelog, every model family has its own shortcut, and it remembers the variant you last selected within that family – if you call `/opus` again, you land on exactly the Opus variant you used last.

The command can be turned off: under "Model slash commands" in `/config` you can disable model shortcuts like `/opus` if they get in your way. Note: `/opus` doesn't appear in the current main reference table of slash commands (cursor.com/docs/cli/reference/slash-commands) – so far the command is only documented in the CLI changelog from July 6, 2026, which doesn't specify which concrete models belong to the Opus family.

whenGood.title: Quickly switch to an Opus model
whenGood.example: /opus

whenGood.title: Return to the last used Opus variant
whenGood.example: /opus – without a detour through the model picker, because the shortcut remembers the last selected Opus variant

whenBad.title: Choose a model from another family
whenBad.why: According to the changelog, /opus only jumps to the Opus family, you can't reach other models through it.
whenBad.alternative: /model for the full selection

commands.name: /composer
commands.summary: Jumps straight to the Composer model family without opening the picker.
commands.what:
`/composer` is a model shortcut: the command jumps directly to Cursor's Composer model family, without opening the regular model picker. This saves you the intermediate step via `/model` and navigating through the list of all available models.

According to Cursor's changelog, the shortcut remembers your last-chosen variant within the Composer family – calling `/composer` again takes you back to that variant instead of a default value. New CLI sessions start with Composer 2.5 as the default model anyway.

Such model shortcuts (e.g. also `/opus`) can be disabled if needed: under "Model slash commands" in `/config`, you can hide them if they get in your way while typing prompts, or if you simply don't need them.

`/composer` so far only appears in the official changelog, not in the main reference table of slash commands.

whenGood.title: Quickly switch to a Composer model without searching the picker
whenGood.example: /composer — right before a new prompt, when you know you want to work with Composer

whenGood.title: Return to the most recently used Composer variant
whenGood.example: Call /composer again after having switched to a different model like /opus in the meantime

whenBad.title: Choosing a model from a different family
whenBad.why: /composer jumps exclusively within the Composer family, not to models from other providers.
whenBad.alternative: Use /model for the full model list

whenBad.title: The shortcuts get in the way when typing prompts that happen to start with a slash
whenBad.why: Model shortcuts like /composer are active by default and react immediately to the input.
whenBad.alternative: Disable shortcuts under "Model slash commands" in /config

commands.name: /fast
commands.summary: Toggles Fast mode, when the current model supports it.
commands.what:
`/fast` switches to a faster response tier, provided the currently active model supports this Fast mode according to the docs. The command doesn't select a model itself, but acts additionally on the model that's already set – whether Fast is actually available depends on the model currently running.

Like the model family shortcuts (e.g. `/opus`), `/fast` can be disabled under "Model slash commands" in `/config` if you don't want to trigger the toggle via command. `/fast` also isn't in the main reference table of slash commands on the Cursor docs page yet, but is only documented via the CLI changelog entry from July 6, 2026, which introduces it together with `/opus` and the other model shortcuts.

whenGood.title: Respond faster with a supported model
whenGood.example: /fast

whenGood.title: Activate Fast mode for a quick follow-up question
whenGood.example: /fast, before asking a quick clarifying question that doesn't need deep analysis

whenBad.title: The current model doesn't support Fast mode
whenBad.why: According to the docs, /fast only has an effect if the model offers the mode.
whenBad.alternative: choose a model that supports Fast
